A shukenja is a wandering priest or monk who has chosen a life of hardship and poverty. That sacrifice, with his deep faith, puts him outside the caste system, and everyone from samurai to peasant treats him with respect. In return he usually gives spiritual and physical help, and teaching, to those who want or need it. He has some fighting training, but his armor and weapons are limited; his main power is his spells, which enlighten, help and protect himself and others.

Requirements

  • Main ability wisdom. Minimum wisdom 12, and strength and constitution 9.
  • Wisdom and constitution both 15 or more give +10% to all experience.
  • Must be good (lawful, neutral or chaotic).

Wisdom

The shukenja's wisdom table (OA Table 27) is the same as the PHB cleric's: bonus spells of one 1st level spell at wisdom 13 and another at 14, one 2nd level spell at 15 and another at 16, one 3rd level spell at 17 and one 4th level spell at 18; a chance of spell failure of 20% at wisdom 9, 15% at 10, 10% at 11, 5% at 12 and none from 13. A shukenja needs wisdom 17 to cast 6th level spells and 18 for 7th level spells.

  • Shukenja and sohei with high wisdom get the bonus spells, but only at spell levels they can already cast. The bonuses add up: a shukenja with wisdom 15 has two extra 1st level spells and one extra 2nd level spell, though he can't cast the 2nd level one until he reaches 4th level.
  • Chance of spell failure is the chance that a spell has no effect at all. Roll every time a spell is cast; on that number or less the spell is used up and fails completely.

Religion

A shukenja serves a religion, but the player needn't pick one. All religions are respected and honored, and common people mix the practices and beliefs of one with another. Unlike the West, the Eastern Lands have no separate, organized church. Faith and ritual are woven into daily life. Temples are everywhere, each more or less independent, whatever god or gods it serves.

Hit points, combat and gear

  • Six-sided hit dice, one a level. Cleric combat and saving throw tables.
  • Armor no heavier than studded leather, though some single pieces of armor are allowed, and limited weapons (see Table 13 on the Classes page).
  • Six proficiency slots at 1st level, only two of them weapons. Of the other four, one must be religion and one calligraphy; the last two can be any nonweapon proficiency.

Training

Before he sets out, a shukenja trains at a monastery or temple in three things: ritual, meditation and self-defense.

  • Ritual: he can perform marriages, christenings, funerals, holy day observances and purifications. A purification can lift curses and ward off evil. He has a 5% chance per level to remove any curse with a purification. To ward off evil, he sanctifies an area of 5 feet radius (75 square feet). At the end of the ritual, everyone in it gets +1 to hit and on saving throws when fighting evil spirits, as long as the shukenja stays inside the purified circle. Several purifications don't add together.
  • Meditation: deep concentration that restores his energy. An hour of unbroken meditation is as restful as two hours' sleep. While meditating he ignores hunger, thirst, heat and cold, but stays conscious and aware, so he suffers no penalty to surprise or initiative.
  • Self-defense: a free proficiency in one unarmed fighting style of the player's choice, not using one of his starting slots.

Ki power

A shukenja can focus his ki to resist an attack in body and mind, gaining +3 on a saving throw. He can do this as many times a day as his level, and may decide at any point in a round, but not after the saving throw is rolled; once the die is rolled, the result stands.

Experience

  • Shukenja aren't warriors, so they earn only half experience for killing or defeating humans and monsters, but full experience for defeating evil spirits.
  • Sworn to poverty, they earn experience for treasure only when it is given to charity or the poor.
  • Unlike others, they earn experience for using healing and curing spells on others: 100 points per spell level used to heal, cure or similarly aid an NPC or creature not connected with the party.

Rules of conduct

A shukenja's religion forbids him to eat meat, requires him to avoid violence (especially killing) whenever he can, and forbids excess in drinking and eating. Breaking these rules brings a punishment chosen by the DM, typically loss of spell levels, loss of honor or a special penance. Sometimes a shukenja is forced to break them; the DM should take that into account when choosing a punishment. A particular religion may add other rules, at the DM's discretion.

Family and honor

Entering religious life, a shukenja cuts all ties to his past. He needn't belong to a family or clan, and doesn't roll on Table 38 (Character Birth); such things belong to the everyday world and matter little to him. He also cares less about honor than others, and is exempt from many honor penalties and bonuses. He does have honor, but it seldom climbs as high as other characters'.

Learning spells

A wu jen's intelligence table (OA Table 32) is the same as the PHB magic-user's: chance to know each listed spell 35% at intelligence 9, 45% at 10-12, 55% at 13-14, 65% at 15-16, 75% at 17, 85% at 18 and 95% at 19 or more; minimum spells per level 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10; maximum 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 18 and all. Check only the spells of levels he can learn, and each new level as he becomes able to cast it.

  • Chance to know: the chance he can learn a given spell. When the character is made, check each spell once, in any order the player likes, so he can check the spells he wants most first. On the chance or less he understands the spell and can learn and cast it. He still has to find a written copy, learn it from someone who knows it, or research it. Each time he becomes able to cast a new level of spells, check each spell of that level.
  • Minimum spells per level: if after one full pass through the list he understands fewer than this many, he goes through again, checking the ones he missed, until he reaches the minimum.
  • Maximum spells per level: once he understands this many spells of a level, he can't check any more of that level.
  • Understanding, knowing and remembering a spell are three different things. Understanding means he can grasp how it works when it is first described to him, spoken or written. Once someone explains it and he understands it, he knows it and can write it in his spell book. Even then he can't cast it until he studies it in his book and memorizes its details.
  • Example: Hideyori, a 1st level wu jen with intelligence 16, has a 65% chance to understand any spell, and can know at least seven and at most 11 of each level. The player picks the spell he wants most, cloud ladder, and rolls 32, so Hideyori understands it, though he can't cast it until someone teaches it to him. The player goes on until Hideyori understands 11 spells or every spell has been checked once. After one pass Hideyori understands 10, which is over his minimum, so he can't check any spell twice. But since he may understand 11 1st level spells, if he comes across another (on a lost scroll or in a borrowed spell book) he can check it.
  • If his intelligence drops for more than a short while, roll for each spell he understands, in any order; a roll over his chance means he no longer understands it. Keep going until he has forgotten enough to fit his new maximum. If his intelligence rises and his maximum goes up, he can try to understand new spells as he finds them.
  • New spells can be learned from a teacher, another wu jen's books (though few wu jen will lend such a treasure) or a magic scroll, which is destroyed in the process.

Ki powers

To learn his spells a wu jen follows a strict mental discipline. He learns to meditate as a shukenja and develops two ki powers, each usable once a day:

  • Sudden action: focusing his ki, he bursts into action, with +3 on initiative for one round, which makes him dangerous in a critical fight.
  • Maximum effect (4th level): he summons great magical energy to cast one spell at least three levels below his own level at maximum effect: maximum range (if he wants it), duration and effect. A 4th level wu jen can cast a 1st level spell this way.

Mastering an element

Wu jen spells fall into five elements: earth/metal, water, fire, wind and wood/nature. A wu jen who has learned every spell of one element up to the highest level he can cast is a master of that element. His spells of that element then give a −1 penalty to saving throws against them and do +1 damage, and he gets +1 on his own saving throws against spells of that element. When he becomes able to cast a higher level, he is no longer a master until he learns all of that element's spells at the new level.

Pupils and strongholds

At 10th level a wu jen draws 1d4 pupils, all 1st level wu jen, who serve him faithfully until they reach half his level and then leave. Each one who leaves is replaced by another 1st level wu jen who wants to study with the master. A wu jen draws no bodies of fighting men, but he can hire them and build a stronghold; not being a warrior, he must also hire a lieutenant to command them.

Languages

Wu jen speak the languages of tengu and oni. Their dealings with these creatures give them +20% on reaction rolls when they meet them.

Family and honor

Like a shukenja, a wu jen has given his life to one goal that demands great mental discipline, and must give up his family ties and his concern for honor. Wu jen needn't roll on Table 38 (Character Birth) and never gain the benefits or suffer the penalties of family and clan. They have integrity, but care little for the codes of honor that obsess samurai and others; honor bonuses and penalties are much smaller for them.

Taboos

Because their power comes from supernatural sources, wu jen live under taboos that don't affect anyone else. They may seem silly or unimportant to others, but they are vital to a wu jen: breaking one brings loss of spells, illness or other misfortune. A wu jen has one taboo at 1st level and takes another for every five levels he gains. The player chooses, and if he suggests a fitting new taboo, the DM should allow it. The DM may also invent others, as long as they are as restrictive. Some examples:

  • Can't eat meat.
  • Can't have more treasure than he can carry.
  • Must make a daily offering (of food, flowers, incense and so on) to one or more spirit powers.
  • Can't bathe.
  • Can't cut his hair.
  • Can't touch a dead body.
  • Can't drink alcohol.
  • Can't wear cloth of a certain color.
  • Can't light a fire.
  • Can't sit facing east (or north, south and so on).

Contacts

Contacts are NPCs who give the yakuza special information and help. They won't adventure with him, but will buy stolen goods, hide him, carry messages and pass on information. They never do anything that puts them in danger, though they may risk their reputations. They stay helpful, and quiet about his doings and their part in them, as long as they are treated fairly, not threatened and not implicated in anything.

  • A yakuza has one contact for every two levels.
  • Contacts aren't set in advance by the DM or a table. When the player wants to use one, he names the contact and his position and tells the DM, who decides whether it fits. The contact can be no more than four levels above the yakuza, and the yakuza must have had some believable reason to meet him in the past.
  • If the DM accepts the contact, his details go on the character sheet and one of the yakuza's available contacts is used up. After that he can use the contact again whenever he needs. (The DM may note details and give the contact a fitting personality.) The player keeps track of his contacts' names.
  • Examples of suitable contacts: a ward's gatekeeper, a ship's captain, a minor samurai in a lord's service, a district magistrate, a rich merchant. In the end it is the DM's judgment.

Ki power and dealing with people

  • Ki: by focusing his energy, he senses and anticipates an opponent's moves for a moment, and shifts to lessen the danger of an attack (sidestepping at the last instant, partly blocking the target and so on). It doesn't stop the attack, but halves the damage he takes (rounding up). Usable once a round, as many times a day as his level.
  • Dealing with people: a successful yakuza soon masters knowing when to threaten, coax, befriend, bribe or persuade. He gets +10% on encounter reaction rolls, except where social standing is involved.

The yakuza family

A yakuza's family isn't his natural one. On becoming a yakuza he is adopted into a yakuza organization (kumi), which works just like a family clan: a family head (oyabun), uncles, fathers and brothers. He is expected to treat them as blood relatives, and some may be. Since it isn't a true family, he doesn't roll on Table 39 (Ancestry) or Table 40 (Birthrights). The family does have honor (Zingi), which must be kept, with all the usual consequences and limits.

  • Stipend: each month he receives 2 ch'ien per level from the family.
  • Brethren (2nd level): he can call on some of his brethren (kyodai-bun) to help in an undertaking, once per level. He may call up to his level in brethren, but needn't call them all. They must be at least one level below him and never above 8th level. Once called, no more can be called until his next level. Major undertakings must be approved by the oyabun.
  • Territory: every yakuza family has a base of operations, its territory, which it guards jealously as the source of its income and power. Families wage secret wars and feuds to keep or seize a district of a city. Since these territories aren't official lands, they can exist inside other states. The center is wherever the family head keeps his headquarters. A new yakuza is given a small part of the territory, and is responsible for more as he rises.
  • Tattoos: yakuza show membership and rank with tattoos. He starts with a small tattoo on his arm, and each new level adds another part of his body. The face, hands and feet are never tattooed, but high-level yakuza have their whole back, chest and arms covered. Everyone knows what the tattoos mean and soon learns not to bother such a person.

Honor and the law

Honor matters to a yakuza, but as a man of the underworld he follows a different code from the samurai's. If his honor falls below his family's, he is thrown out of the family, though he may later be taken back. While cast out he is treated as a non-person: no one in the territory will speak to him or help him in any way, for fear of revenge. His family won't avenge his death, though other yakuza families still treat him as an enemy.

Though the government sometimes tolerates, allows or even recognizes them, yakuza are still criminals. They can always be arrested and punished for their crimes, from prison to humiliating execution, and must always beware the law. Because of this it pays the family to keep everything in its territory running smoothly and quietly. It strictly controls every undertaking there; superiors oversee all its activities and report to the family head. When a yakuza or a stranger makes trouble in the territory, the family acts quickly and efficiently: the troublemaker may be hunted down and killed, handed to the police or driven off. In this way the family works as an unofficial arm of the police, preventing trouble and lightening the official police's work.

Family matters greatly to most characters. It means not just parents, brothers and sisters, but the whole web of relatives: uncles, grandparents, cousins, great-uncles, aunts and in-laws, called the family or clan in these rules. Knowing one's family, its alliances and its feuds can be vital in the society of the Eastern Lands.

The family also includes its ancestors, especially those who were famous in their day. They are treated with respect and reverence and can bring the family great honor. A warrior often rides into battle calling out his ancestors' deeds as proof of his own worth; an official holds up his ancestors as shining examples. Someone who doesn't know his family and its past is often not thought a whole person.

Some classes don't need families, because their profession has become their new family. A shukenja, for example, is expected to cut every tie with his past, which would stand in the way of his spiritual purity. Players may give such characters a family background, but then must follow the family and clan rules.

Family structure

Next, outline the family: the head of the clan, uncles, brothers and so on. The player needs a copy of the Family Chart (book p.144), which has three rows, one per generation. The top row, “Head of Family,” has places for the head of the family, the character's grandfather, and his great-aunts and great-uncles. The middle row, “Father,” is for the father, uncles and aunts. The bottom row, “Children,” is the character's own generation: him and his brothers and sisters.

  1. Every family has a head: a venerable (usually old) man who founded the clan, always in place 1 of the top row. He may be related to other families not shown (making everyone in both distant kin), which the DM decides. Every branch traces its descent to him.
  2. For each row, roll 1d8: that many places are used, and the rest are crossed out starting from the highest number. For example, a 5 on the top row crosses out places 8, 7 and 6: the character has a grandfather and four great-uncles or great-aunts.
  3. Then find the character's line. Starting with the top row, roll the die closest to the number of places used without being smaller (five places, roll 1d6). That place is the grandfather (reroll if the roll is higher than the places used); everyone else on the row is his brother or sister. Do the same for the father's row and the character's own row (his order of birth). Lines can be drawn between them to make a family tree.
  4. Each place has lines for sex, name and number of children. Each place has a 70% chance of being male; the head of the family, the grandfather and the father are always male. Everyone carries the family name, man or woman, usually written and spoken before the personal name, since the family matters more than the person.
  5. Each place has 1d8−2 children; zero or less means that branch has no offspring. Only the branch leading to the character needs a chart; filling it in gives a sense of the clan's size and shape.

More detailed families

This method gives a simplified picture of how a family grows. Those who want more detail can add any of the following, though it takes longer, and players may want to fill in the family gradually.

  • Marriages: each woman of the clan is married on a 1-5 on 1d6 (staying single was rare and unwanted), though player characters never have to marry. Marriages are usually outside the clan, though distant relatives sometimes marry. A marriage widens the family, giving the character NPC relatives in other clans, but ties by marriage are much weaker than blood ties: related families usually get along, but distant cousins aren't guaranteed friends. NPCs of a family related by marriage give +10% on reactions. The DM decides which family is linked, usually one of about equal rank, and notes it on the master family chart; the player notes it on his Family Chart.
  • Adoptions: anyone on the chart has a 1 in 20 (5%) chance of having been adopted. On a 1 or 2 on 1d6 he was an orphan, related only to his adoptive clan. Others were adopted while their own clan, even their parents, still lived, and so have two clans, birth and adoptive. Like marriages, adoptions widen the family's ties and give +10% on reactions with the adoptive clan. Unlike marriages, they often cross birth ranks, and are often political, letting a lower family raise its status.
  • Polygamy: having several wives at once is legal and known, though most marriages have one wife. It is common only in very rich and powerful families, who use marriage to secure alliances and control other families. The DM should think carefully before allowing it. If he does, he decides whether the grandfather or father had several wives (others don't matter), how many children each bore, and where the character stands. It greatly tangles relationships. Usually the first (principal) wife is favored and only her children can inherit directly, but the father might favor a later wife's children (more talented, or their mother more loved), or the first wife might bear only daughters while the first son comes from a later wife. Each wife usually schemes against the others for her children's sake, and their relatives get involved: the first wife's family may be insulted by slights to her and her children, while powerful relatives may press the husband to take another wife. The results vary so much that the DM must decide them. As a rule the first son of the first wife inherits and the other wives' children get little or nothing; if not, the first wife's family reacts badly to the other children. Most marriages probably stay with one wife simply because husbands want to avoid these troubles.
  • Further generations: the chart covers only three generations. Players may add earlier ones the same way. They add color but have little effect on play; in the end everyone in the campaign may turn out to be related. This adds history but no reaction bonuses, since families drift apart over the generations.
  • Related player characters: with the DM's agreement, player characters may belong to the same clan (not necessarily the same father or grandfather). They must be the same race. Barbarian player characters can share a family only with other barbarians, and samurai only with other samurai. Related characters have the same birth rank and the same number of places on the top row. After that they roll normally, but the key details of both charts must match: the same relatives with the same numbers of children, and the same names. Two characters can't hold the same place (both first son of the same father) unless they are twins, and even then one is older. Only one set of ancestry rolls is made, and ancestral holdings are assigned the same way on both charts. Related characters can make for colorful campaigns.
  • Deaths: once a game year (besides any random events), the DM checks whether NPC family members die of natural causes or accidents: 10% for each on the top row, 7% on the father's row and 5% on the children's row. A dead NPC is crossed off. His possessions go to his first son 75% of the time; otherwise there is a power struggle: roll percentile dice for each of his brothers, each of his surviving children and the head of the family, and the highest roll gets the inheritance (an odd will, or fighting over the property). This almost always causes bad feeling, feuds and perhaps a split in the clan, as the DM decides. If the head of the family dies, the title passes to his next brother, or if none survives, to his eldest son; this too can cause bad feeling or break up the clan.
  • Replacing a dead character: if a player character dies, the player may return as one of his brothers or sisters. The new character can't hold any property but gets normal birthright rolls, and starts at 1st level.

Put the emperor or supreme ruler at the center, and give each family in the campaign a place: high-ranking families close to the emperor, low-ranking ones farther out. Connect clans related by marriage with a dashed line, by blood with a solid line, ancestral allies with a dotted line and ancestral enemies with a line of arrows.

What the results mean

  • Advantageous marriage: recently the family married one of its daughters to a man 1-3 social levels higher, and is now related by marriage to a higher class.
  • Ancestral alliance: a long friendship with another family of about the same level, chosen by the DM. NPC encounter reactions between the two families get +20%.
  • Ancestral feud: a long blood feud with another family of about the same level, chosen by the DM. Reactions between them get −40%, and poor reactions lead to insults, duels or attacks.
  • Brilliant artisan: the family produced a craftsman famous for very fine work.
  • Castle: one branch holds the deed to a castle or the like (a barbarian clan might hold a natural stronghold or a semi-permanent camp), with the fighting men to garrison it and guard the commoners who live nearby and serve its lord.
  • Classic artist: a distant ancestor was an artist whose work is now a classic of its kind.
  • Common bloodline and traditional business: the book doesn't describe these.
  • Criminal: a recent ancestor was a notorious condemned criminal (horse thief, murderer and so on), a terrible stain on the family's honor.
  • Curse: an old curse haunts the family, perhaps for some great evil done long ago: a vengeful spirit, men who tend to die young and so on. Everyone knows of it. It doesn't affect family members' daily lives or the player character directly, but a quest to lift it can make an exciting adventure.
  • Defeated family: the family was once large and powerful but lost a great struggle for power, a lasting dishonor. It has an ancestral feud with the winning family (chosen by the DM), and ancestral alliances with any other defeated families.
  • Estate: the family holds the deed to an estate, with the peasants who work it, warriors to defend it and a fitting house for the owner. For barbarians it can instead be a large herd. An estate earns its owner 100 to 1,000 ch'ien a year.
  • Famous general, holy man or minister: an ancestor remembered for heroism in war, religious purity, or wisdom as a counselor, minister, adviser or chief. The family reveres him and others know of him.
  • Folk hero: a distant ancestor was a hero and defender of common people, who still remember. NPC commoners give the family +10% on encounter reactions.
  • Great betrayal: a distant ancestor tried (and failed) to commit a great treachery against his lord. His name is only spoken with loathing.
  • Great hero: a distant ancestor was a hero of folklore and legend, whose deeds (grander with every telling) have made him the model of a hero. Everyone knows his name, family and deeds.
  • Hereditary title: the head of the family holds a hereditary title of respect or nobility, which passes to his son when he dies.
  • Imperial bloodline: the family has some blood tie to the imperial house (or the land's highest ruler). However thin, it gives some claim to the throne, though no one in the family is likely ever to sit on it, with so many claimants of better blood (such as the emperor's children).
  • Infamous general or minister: the family produced a leader known for greed, bungling, stupidity or corruption. Since he rose high, his misdeeds or failures are known to all.
  • Land: the family holds title to land. Mountain land is poor and can't be farmed, though bamboo and lumber can be taken from it; it supports only 2-8 people (one small family). Farm land grows crops, mostly rice: small farms support 3-12 people and moderate farms 4-16. Town land may mean a whole village, a mansion in town or several city blocks. Land earns income for the branch that holds it, depending on its size. If the family holds only one piece of land, some branch lives on it and works it; if more, the family doesn't live on the land but collects rent from commoners who do. Land earns 10 to 2,000 ch'ien a year.
  • Merchant fleet: a branch of the family has a successful trading business with 2-5 ships (caravans inland) and warehouses, and hires sailors (or teamsters), guards, clerks and so on. It earns 100 to 1,000 ch'ien a year.
  • Notorious moneylender: a recent ancestor got rich lending money to local people, usually at outrageous interest. The family has a bad name but more wealth: the character gets an extra roll on Table 40 (Birthrights).
  • Roll again: roll again with the next larger die (d4 becomes d6, d6 becomes d8 and so on); if already rolling d100, add 10 to the roll instead.
  • Secret society: the family has long ties to a secret society, whose purpose the DM decides. No one outside the family and the society knows, but it gives the character contacts inside the society.
  • Tragic event: some sad event befell a distant ancestor, in love, war or business, but the nobility of his suffering has actually raised the family's honor. Such tales often become folktales, plays or songs.

In the Eastern Lands, power, wealth and position mean nothing to a character without honor. Honor reflects his character and his family's: his worth in society, his reliability, his decency, how far he can be trusted, and more. A family's honor affects the character's, and the reverse. Honor brings respect, power, influence and position; without it come disrespect, humiliation and insults.

A character earns honor by his deeds, like experience, and can lose it by them too, and honor is easier to lose than to gain, so characters must weigh what they do. Breaking faith, treachery, cowardice and unavenged insults cost honor; brave deeds, self-sacrifice, mastery of skills and keeping faith earn it. As honor rises, the character gets better reactions, gifts, and better characters to replace honorable ones who die.

This honor isn't a paladin's or cavalier's. It doesn't judge good and evil: high honor doesn't make a character good, nor low honor evil. A cruel villain can have high honor, and a heroic samurai, through bad luck, low honor. Honor measures what the character and his clan have accomplished: obedience, loyalty, talent and success, which anyone of any alignment can have.

Players record their characters' honor points. At the end of each adventure or major encounter, the DM gives honor to characters who carried themselves well and takes it from those who acted dishonorably. Unlike experience, honor isn't earned on every adventure; it takes something special to gain or lose it.

Then add the honor from birthrights (Table 40), and finally the character's lowest ability score. This is his starting honor; write it as Character Honor.

Gaining and losing honor

A character's deeds in play gain or lose him honor. Some classes care more about honor than others and gain or lose more for the same deed; a samurai's honor swings far more than a wu jen's or a shukenja's. No character can have more than 100 honor.

The DM always awards honor. Players may reasonably protest if they think he missed something, but his decision is final. Honor is normally awarded at the end of an adventure, though on long adventures the DM may award it after a major encounter or deed, or at the end of each session. Typical awards are on the Honor Awards page. No list can cover everything; the DM uses it as a guide in other situations.

Changing the family's honor

One character's deeds can raise or lower his whole clan. Noble, heroic, successful characters lift their family's name; cowardly, lying, treacherous ones drag it down with them.

  • When a character's honor is 10 points above his family's, the family's base honor rises by one. The same happens at 20, 30, 40 and so on above it, each group of 10 only once.
  • This can still happen when the character is already at the most honor he can have. Then honor awards count only toward raising the family: the character has reached his peak, but his deeds still bring credit to his clan.
  • A character who loses five or more honor for a single deed lowers his family's base honor by one: his shameful behavior is a lasting stain on the family name.
  • Whenever a character changes the family's honor, every other family member's honor rises or falls by the same amount, so family members' deeds affect one another.

Effects of honor

  • Below zero: any character of any race or class whose honor falls below zero is out of the game. Tear up the record sheet.
  • Samurai and kensai: a samurai or kensai whose honor falls below his family's current base honor loses his status (the samurai becomes a ronin, the kensai is treated as a bushi). He has dishonored his family.
  • Below the family or class: a character of any class whose honor falls below his family's honor, or below his class's base, gets −20% on all reactions with members of his family, until his honor again equals or passes theirs.
  • Above the family or class: for every 10 points above his family's or class's base honor, he gets +5% on reactions with members of the same family or organization. But as his honor rises, so does his family's or group's, so they become harder and harder to impress.
  • 75 honor: a powerful lord he knows (a daimyo, an important official and so on) sends him a gift suited to his level and class: an ornate sword scabbard for a 6th level samurai, perhaps a miscellaneous magic item for a 12th level wu jen. The lord never gives anything that could threaten himself. The character is expected to return the courtesy somehow.
  • 80 honor: his name starts turning up in popular songs and stories as a minor or local hero. Each week there is a 10% chance that a notorious foe (human or not) starts boasting he can beat the character, and the boasts always reach the character's ears. If he won't seek out and defeat the boaster, he loses 10 honor.
  • 90 honor: one of the most powerful lords of the land (the DM decides who) invites him to serve. He needn't accept, but refusing angers the lord, and he gets −10% on all reactions with that lord and his followers from then on.
  • 95 honor: he is a great hero, fit for epic songs and long folktales. He gets +10% on all reactions with those of lower rank, and −10% with creatures of opposite alignment or belief: those inclined to like him respect him more, and those who dislike him hate him all the more for his greatness.
  • After death: when a character dies and isn't brought back, the player's next character gets a bonus. Subtract the family's or class's base honor from the character's honor at death (including any honor for dying gloriously), divide by 10 and round down. That many bonus points can be added to the new character's ability score or hit point rolls as the player likes, but no more than three to any one roll, and never raising a roll above the race or class maximum. The points can't be saved for later. The new character may be of any race, class or family, as long as he meets the ability score requirements normally.

Everyone in the Eastern Lands needs money, and nobles need a great deal of it. A noble is expected to support the arts, field armies, provide for his followers, build public works, keep a household that suits his rank, and give gifts on many occasions. Lesser folk need money too, for new clothes, better equipment, new lodgings and their own tastes, all of which improve a character's standing.

The Eastern Lands are broad, with many cultures and traditions, and money works differently from place to place. The great empire of Shou Lung has a strong central government and can do what perhaps no one else in the world can: print paper money. T'u Lung, loosely held together, mints regular coins, while the empire of Kozakura, emperor in name only, freely uses other lands' coins. Out at the edges of civilization, warlords sometimes mint coins, and beyond them barbarian tribes may live their whole lives without seeing a coin, trading by barter alone.

Four kinds of money system

  • Established currency: the government controls the minting, so coins are uniform in size and shape. Melting coins down gives less than their face value. Merchants accept them because the imperial treasury backs them and everyone knows what a coin will buy in rice, fish, cloth or work. That trust lets the government issue paper money worth far more than the paper. Officials may oversee market prices to stop them rising. Barter is uncommon but still used, and taxes can be paid in grain and similar goods. Expect haggling over larger purchases.
  • Regular currency and barter: coins are minted and used, though not always regular in size or shape. A coin is worth the metal in it: a silver coin's value depends on the price of silver and how much the coin holds. Weighing coins is common. Larger purchases are often made by barter, trading goods of equal value; land may be bought with gems, art, services, or a share of a crop for a time. Prices swing widely, so haggling is common.
  • Irregular currency and barter: coins may or may not be minted, and if they are, they are often irregular. Foreign coins are used freely. Every coin is worth only its metal, and paper money is useless. Most things are bought by barter, with rough standard values (a sheep is worth so much, a horse about so much). The rice a man harvests or collects in a year is his wealth. Since barter goods are bulky, people write contracts signing over part of a future harvest. A man's wealth is the goods he owns, the goods he can make or grow, and the contracts he holds, and the law exists to make people honor contracts and obligations.
  • Pure barter: wealth is only the goods a man owns and can trade. This is most common in the uncivilized lands. Contracts, written or spoken, are rare. A buyer pays with goods of equal value, and haggling is a must, since nothing has a set value: an item is worth what the buyer will give and the seller will accept. Laws are informal, and a man's name as an honest dealer, a cheat, a fool, a liar or a hard bargainer greatly affects what others will pay him or ask of him.

Characters normally deal with only one of these systems unless they travel far. Which one depends on where the campaign is set, and the DM can choose whichever system is simplest so play isn't slowed down.

Coins

Elsewhere in the game, coins are copper, silver and gold. In the Eastern Lands, money is copper, silver and paper. Gold is valuable, but it isn't proper currency; it is kept for art and craftwork.

The coin names below can be used anywhere in the Eastern Lands. The DM can change their values from land to land for rates of exchange or how much a coin is wanted.

  • Fen and yuan (copper): the most common coins. The fen is the lowest; a yuan equals five fen. Each coin has a hole through the center, and coins are threaded on strings, usually 50 to 100 to a string. These cash strings are carried tucked in the sleeve, which makes coins easy to carry and count.
  • Ch'ao (paper): a paper note. One ch'ao equals 100 fen or 20 yuan. The most common notes are for one, ten and 100 ch'ao. Paper is easy to handle, so people prefer it for amounts of 100 fen or more.
  • Tael and ch'ien (silver): the tael is a pierced coin like the fen, often carried on cash strings; one tael equals 100 fen, 20 yuan, or one ch'ao. The ch'ien is a small bar or miniature ingot worth 10 ch'ao, 10 tael, 200 yuan or 1,000 fen. Ch'ien are awkward to carry and rarely used day to day; people hoard them for times when copper and paper money lose value.

Gajin money and rates of exchange

If the campaign includes contact with the gajin (foreigners), sooner or later characters will carry money between the gajin lands and the Eastern Lands, and since the coins differ, everyone needs exchange rates. Along established caravan routes and in major trading ports, moneylenders change one kind of coin for the other.

Spending foreign money in the Eastern Lands:

  • Gold coins can't be spent, since gold isn't currency, but they can be sold as gold at the going price, typically 2-7 tael per gold piece. The price depends on how much gold is on the market, how pure it is (gold coins usually aren't very pure), and how much the character sells; selling a lot at once floods the market and drives the price down.
  • Foreign silver coins are smaller and poorer than local ones, and merchants don't want them. A character normally gets 8 to 13 (1d6+7) fen for each silver piece.
  • Copper pieces are closer to standard: one fen for every two copper pieces.

Taking money out of the Eastern Lands:

  • Ch'ao are worthless outside the Eastern Lands except as curiosities (and worthless in some parts of the Eastern Lands too). A character heading for gajin lands should change his ch'ao into something solid first.
  • Lands with established currency try to keep their coins at home, since coins leaving the country hurt the economy. Exporting coins counts as smuggling and is a crime.
  • Characters who manage it anyway find the coins readily accepted, since other lands lack a strong currency. One fen equals one copper piece, and a yuan also equals one copper piece. The text says a tael generally fetches 4-14 (2d6+2) silver pieces, but Table 46 prints 2-12 silver pieces; both are as printed. A ch'ien is worth 2-8 gold pieces.

The katana and the daisho

For a samurai, the katana is more than a sword: it is part of his honor and his family's. It is his personal weapon, not for others to use. Touching the scabbard of his sheathed katana insults him, and so does drawing the blade without his permission. A katana may have been in a family for generations, and losing it is a disgrace that only recovering the sword and punishing the takers can wipe away; many samurai have died trying. The price on the list is for an average blade; others cost more or less with their quality, workmanship and history.

A wakizashi that is part of a matched set is treated the same way. The katana and wakizashi worn together are the daisho ("long and short"), and in many lands of the Eastern Lands they mark a samurai's rank: only samurai may wear both. Anyone else who does can be arrested or executed on the spot for claiming a rank he has no right to.

The Eastern Lands are warm: steaming jungles, humid forests and blistering steppes. A man sealed in metal could cook inside it, or watch his armor rust until the joints lock, the hinge pins shear and the plates rot away. It is also a land that prizes speed: the steppe rider who strikes suddenly, the ninja slipping unseen through a camp, the samurai who falls from his horse and lands on his feet, the monk who strikes fast and dodges every blow. A warrior's speed counts for more than heavy protection.

So armor here is made to resist the weather, move freely, stay light, and look colorful and artistic. Heavy metal armor such as field plate is seldom seen. Armorers work instead in leather, brigandine, mail and lamellar (laced) construction.

  • The most common armor is cloth and leather. Foot soldiers wear quilted cotton or padded leather. Higher-ranking warriors may have hardened leather scale or brigandine.
  • Chain mail is often worn hidden under clothing, or sewn in among rich silks and soft dyed leathers.
  • Now and then a noble has armor of metal bands. Solid iron and steel are kept for helmets and vital areas.
  • Laced armor is made of small metal plates tied together with colored leather lacing, then carefully lacquered against damp. It is colorful, elaborate and painfully slow to make. The lacings form rows of bright patterns; sections may be covered with painted leather, edges trimmed in red copper, and each part tied down with red silk cords to sculpted bosses of copper, silver or gold. Each piece is a work of art, and complete sets are rare, being so costly and slow to make.

Suits and pieces

In OA, all armor is either a suit or a piece.

  • A suit is a complete set that protects the whole body. The most common are padded, leather, studded leather, leather scale, chain mail and brigandine. Metal scale, splint mail, banded mail and laced suits are rare. Plate mail, field plate and full plate are virtually unknown.
  • Pieces are made of laced armor in many shapes and colors, and each protects part of the body.

Grenades

Ninja often carry grenades. They don't explode with force: they are blown-out eggshells (or hollowed nutshells, or paper packets) filled with powders, used to blind foes and cause distractions.

  • Throwing one takes a normal to-hit roll, using the rules for grenade-like missiles to find where a miss lands. Armor doesn't change the roll, since the powder bursts into a small cloud on impact.
  • Pepper: affects one target, who must save versus poison or be helpless for 1-6 rounds from choking and sneezing.
  • Dust: the same, except the victim is blinded for 1-6 rounds.
  • Flash powder: must be thrown onto a fire, where it flares brilliantly. Everyone looking at the light is blinded for 1-3 rounds. Anyone who may or may not have been looking saves versus petrification to avoid it.
  • Poison smoke: must also be thrown onto a fire. It bursts into vile, stinking smoke that spreads 5 feet by 5 feet a round, up to a 10 foot by 10 foot area per grenade. Everyone in it must save versus poison or be blinded and helpless from the acid stench, and everyone in it takes 1-2 hit points of damage a round. The smoke lasts one turn or until the wind blows it away.
  • Eggshell grenades are fragile and must be packed carefully. If a character carrying them falls 10 feet or more and takes damage, each grenade must save versus crushing blow.

The rate of fire and ranges for grenades are on the Weapons page (Table 51).

Like shields, barding varies from land to land, and even where it is used it is rarely as heavy or complete as in the gajin lands; bad weather and the need for speed limit armor. It is usually seen only on the mounts of important nobles, generals and shock troops.

Weapon proficiencies

  • A character can take a proficiency in any weapon his class allows. It costs one slot, and it is noted on his character sheet.
  • Unarmed combat can't be taken as a weapon proficiency unless the character is studying under a master.
  • A character can pick up and use a weapon his class doesn't allow, but always with his class's non-proficiency penalty (the worst one, for a split class character), and he can't keep and carry it to use later.
  • Some characters can't use some weapons at all, whatever the penalty: a character under 5 feet tall can't use a weapon over 12 feet long; one under 4 feet tall can't use the daikyu (great bow); one weighing less than 100 pounds can't use a heavy crossbow, a two-handed sword, or any weapon weighing more than 200 gp.

Weapon specialization

Only samurai and bushi can specialize. A specialist trains and disciplines himself in one weapon. His dedication isn't as fierce as a kensai's, so he doesn't gain a kensai's abilities, but he can learn other weapons more easily than a kensai.

  • Cost: specializing in a melee weapon or a crossbow costs two slots; in any other missile weapon, three.
  • Bushi: can specialize in any one weapon, chosen when the character is created.
  • Samurai: can specialize only in the katana and the bow, and is the only character who can specialize in two weapons at once. He must specialize in the katana when he is created; he can put off the bow until later.
  • The weapon must be one specific weapon, not a group: a character can specialize in the katana, but not in all swords.

Melee weapons:

  • +1 to hit and +2 damage with the weapon.
  • The character knows iaijutsu (fast draw) with the weapon and gets its benefits (see the iaijutsu proficiency).
  • He uses the next higher row of the Multiple Attacks table with this weapon. A 1st level samurai makes 3/2 attacks a round with his specialized weapon; at 5th level he makes 2.
  • After 1st level, one more slot gives double specialization: +3 to hit and damage.

Bow:

  • The specialist gains a "point blank" range of 5 to 30 feet, besides short, medium and long. At point blank range he is +2 to hit and damage and his base damage is doubled; strength and magic bonuses to damage aren't doubled but are added after.
  • At short range he is +1 to hit. At medium range and beyond he has no special bonus to hit, and beyond point blank range no damage bonus.
  • If he starts the round with an arrow ready (nocked, drawn and aimed at a target), he fires before initiative is rolled.
  • At higher levels he gains more shots, as shown on Table 57.

Crossbow:

  • Point blank range is 5 to 60 feet, with the same benefits as for the bow.
  • +1 to hit and damage at short range; +1 to hit at medium range.
  • The same benefit for having the weapon ready at the start of the round.
  • Extra attacks a round, depending on the kind of crossbow, as shown on Table 57.

Characters are expected to be more than warriors, priests or magicians: to be complete, they must also be skilled in the arts. Among the well-born, contests in poetry, painting and other arts are frequent and popular. Winners gain honor and experience; losers risk humiliation and lost favor. Players do well to make their characters skilled in many things beyond their profession.

The four lists

  • Peaceful proficiencies are grouped as common, artisan, court and barbarian.
  • Only barbarians can learn barbarian proficiencies.
  • The other lists show where a character must be to learn a proficiency, and help the DM choose proficiencies for non-player characters: a peasant knows proficiencies from the common list, a noble from the court list.

Learning

Peaceful proficiencies have no set study time. An adventure doesn't fill every minute of a character's life; there are gaps between adventures and idle hours during them, and he is assumed to spend that time practicing a weapon or polishing a skill.

To learn a proficiency, he needs the tools at hand and, when he first learns it, a place where people skilled in it can train and guide him. To learn poetry, he must have spent time at a court or noble house where poetry is practiced, comparing his work with the masters' and learning proper forms, imagery and subjects. To learn weaponsmithing, he must live among skilled smiths. How much contact with the masters he needs is left to the DM.

The base number

  • Weapon proficiencies improve on their own as the character rises in level; that is built into the combat tables. Peaceful proficiencies don't.
  • Each peaceful proficiency has a base number. Like a to-hit roll, the character must roll that number or more on 1d20 to succeed.
  • The number never improves just because the character rises in level. From 2nd level on, he can spend more slots on the proficiency; each extra slot adds +1 to his roll. There is no limit to the slots he can spend, but after all modifiers he never succeeds on less than 3.
  • Magic items that improve a proficiency help only a character who already knows it; the item's description says how.

Example: the samurai Torimatsu Akimori learns calligraphy, a court proficiency open to samurai, spending the two slots it needs at 1st level. Its base number is 17 in this example (Table 61 prints 18; the compendium uses the table's 18). At 3rd level he spends another slot, and is +1 on the roll, so he succeeds on 16. At 4th level, getting ready for a major contest at court, he spends two more slots: he is now +3 and succeeds on 14.

Success and failure

  • For most peaceful proficiencies there is no clear success or failure. A character who knows a proficiency can use it properly whatever the roll. A farmer doesn't roll to remember how to farm, and a carpenter doesn't fail to build a house because of a bad roll. Usually no roll is needed at all.
  • When the quality of the work matters, roll. Equal to or above the base number means superior work; below means average work, or worse on an exceptionally bad roll. The farmer has a fine, average or poor harvest; the carpenter builds a handsome, well-designed house or one that is drafty and leaks.
  • Some proficiencies, such as weaponsmith and armorer, have a clear success or failure: a botched effort can leave the item useless. These are always rolled, and are marked "Always rolled" in the tables below.

Contests

Contests in the peaceful arts are a regular part of life in the Eastern Lands. Winners gain honor and experience; losers lose honor; and the results can greatly change a character's standing.

  • Formal contests are most often held at court or in noble households and announced ahead of time. Often a subject is set and contestants bring a finished work; sometimes there is none, and the contest tests improvisation. No one has to attend, but those who want their lord's favor or a political post seldom miss a chance to appear at court, and those who stay away lose a little honor, unless circumstances made attending impossible.
  • Informal contests can happen whenever nobles gather. A host watching a beautiful moonrise with his guests may suddenly ask them for a poem about it. Honor gained and lost is less than at a formal contest. Characters should be ready for anything.
  • Who wins: each contestant rolls 1d20 against his number. A failed roll puts him out (he has lost). Keep rolling until one contestant is left; he wins. If everyone fails the first roll, the contest is inauspicious (held on an unlucky day, perhaps): there is no winner, and no one gains or loses honor.
  • Experience for winning: 50 times the host's level for an informal contest, 100 times for a formal one. Honor is on the Honor Awards page.

Optional bonuses

If the DM likes, he can give a one-time bonus for what the player does, not the character. A player who offers an example of the art that fits the moment (a piece of Chinese or Japanese poetry, say) can get +1; one who actually performs it (writes a haiku, for instance) can get +2. This rule is optional, and DMs and players who use it must find their own sources on the forms of these arts.

The proficiency lists

"Slots to learn" is the number of slots it takes to learn the proficiency. After that, each improvement costs one slot, however many it took to learn. Descriptions, with special rules (armorer, bowyer, weaponsmith, tracking, horsemanship, iaijutsu and others), are on each proficiency in the OA Proficiencies compendium.

Spells matter most to shukenja and wu jen, and to a lesser degree to sohei, and they shape play a great deal. Each spell is a particular power, set off by its components:

  • Verbal (V): words the caster speaks. A caster who can't speak can't use these spells.
  • Somatic (S): gestures, mostly of the hands. The caster's hands and arms must be free for the whole casting.
  • Material (M): things that are written on, burned, shaken, tossed in the air and so on. Most are common, but some spells need elaborate preparation. Without the material components, the spell can't be cast at all.

How many spells a character can use depends on his class and level (see his class page). High ability scores and magic items may raise the number.

Shukenja

Spells are the holy man's armor and sword, signs from his deity of the power of his faith and his religion. He shouldn't hold back from using them out of fear of pride.

  • Helper: each spell is a living lesson in the shukenja's calling, and many of them aid, comfort and guide others. Through these services he teaches the noblest values. He should never refuse his services to the needy or unfortunate, nor use them for personal gain, but for the good of his religion. His goal is to give aid and comfort to the weak and helpless, as a living example of his faith, and his experience awards reflect this.
  • Adviser: he also advises and guides others, and many of his spells help find the best course of action, some for the crisis at hand, others giving insight into what the future probably holds. In a party, he is the wise man whose words should be heeded: guide, teacher and sage. His advice isn't always perfect, but others would do well to listen.
  • Protection: the world isn't perfect, so some of his spells protect him, mostly defensively. He doesn't want to crush his foes, but sometimes must, so he has a few offensive spells. They are rarely severely harmful; he has no wish to cause death and anguish.
  • Reversed spells: some spells can be cast for the opposite effect, as the description says. Using some reversed spells can call the shukenja's faith into question. Careless misuse brings his deity's disfavor (loss of levels or experience), and flagrant disregard leads to a change of alignment. The DM decides the final consequences.
  • Getting spells: he meditates for at least six hours, cleansing his mind and preparing himself as a vessel for his deity's purpose, and then chooses his spells. Choosing is part of his training: how can he help others without the foresight to see his own needs? A cast spell is forgotten until he composes his mind again, because the spiritual power passing through him disturbs the harmony of his mind.
  • Sohei use shukenja spells, but only those marked for sohei (see Shukenja Spells).

Wu jen

Spells are the wu jen's main tool: to defend, attack, investigate and research. His spells are often more dangerous and powerful in combat, single or mass, than a shukenja's, but he can do little for the injured, sick and unfortunate beyond a few spells and his own skills. His magic has neither the limits of mercy and kindness nor their benefits.

Common folk often fear him: a man of unknown mysteries who gave up comfort and company to learn secret lore. That lore is taught only by those who already have it, and masters choose pupils carefully for dedication, cleverness and talent, then reveal their secrets slowly and jealously, fearing rivals and misuse.

Students are taken young and spend years in solitude. At first a student is little more than a servant: he rises early, fetches water, cooks his master's meal, spends hours fetching odd items and cleaning, eats his bowl of rice at midday, then meditates for hours (a twitch earns a sharp blow of the master's cane). Then he studies forgotten languages and the secret meanings in everyday words, practices calligraphy with brush and ink (vital to magical work), cooks his master's dinner, studies the ancient classics, and sleeps a few hours well after dark before starting again. As he proves himself, the master teaches him more of the secrets of casting.

  • No spell book: unlike a magic-user, the wu jen keeps no spell book. He has a collection of scrolls and books, classic treatises of lore; each scroll is a commentary on the art and discipline of casting one spell, full of philosophy and metaphysics.
  • Memorizing: the scrolls are complex and exacting and must be studied before any spell is memorized. He needs at least six hours of restful meditation and study with his scrolls. A cast spell is forgotten until memorized again, because the release of mystic energy upsets his delicate mental balance.
  • Starting spells: a new wu jen has just left his master, carrying a few nonmagical scrolls he copied from his master's collection, recording the 1st level spells he knows. Roll 3d6 for how many. If the roll is below the minimum for his intelligence, he has the minimum; if above the maximum, he has the maximum. The player chooses the spells from the list. No percentile roll is needed for these, since his years of apprenticeship trained him in them.
  • New spells: each time he finds a treatise on a spell he doesn't know, roll percentile to see whether he can master it. He can never have fewer than his minimum or more than his maximum spells per level.
  • Reaching a new spell level: the DM picks one of two ways. If master and student are still friendly, the wu jen can return and spend a month studying and copying his master's scrolls, gaining spells as he did at 1st level; the DM can rule that the master lacks some spells (this works best if the DM makes the master a non-player character with a set level and spell list). Or the wu jen must find new spells himself, in other wu jen's scrolls or forgotten on dusty shelves in temples and academies, so he may gain few or none of the new level when he advances. Either way, the DM secretly determines which spells he can learn (based on intelligence), within the minimum and maximum. Players should ask their DM which way is used.

Reading a spell description

Spells are listed by level, alphabetically within each level, in the OA Spells compendium. Each gives its type, level, range, duration, area of effect, components (V, S, M), casting time and saving throw, then a description. Spells that also appear in the PHB or UA are included in short form, so no one has to look through other books.

  • Range is in inches (meaning tens of feet or yards) or "touch". A touch spell means the caster must touch the target. Against an unwilling target he needs an unmodified to-hit roll; if it misses, the spell still goes off but is wasted.
  • Duration is how many turns or rounds the spell lasts. "Permanent" lasts until something removes it, if anything can. "Instantaneous" is a brief flash, almost impossible to avoid.
  • Area of effect is how big an area, or how many creatures, the spell affects.
  • Casting time is in rounds or segments: 10 segments to the round, 10 rounds to the turn.
  • Saving throw says whether a save is allowed, and whether it halves the effect (1/2) or cancels it (neg.).

The properties

  • Armor of quality: not magical, but so finely made that it is light and very flexible. No armor class bonus, but it counts as one encumbrance class lighter than normal. It is decorated with fine taste, worth 2d4 times the normal price. A character with the armorer proficiency can make it (see the proficiency).
  • Etherealness: makes the wearer ethereal, as armor of etherealness in the DMG.
  • Vulnerability: works as armor of vulnerability in the DMG. Its +1, +2, +3 and so on (from Table 76) is really a penalty to the wearer's armor class.
  • Missile attraction: cursed; works like the DMG's missile attractor shield for deciding whether the wearer is the target of a missile attack. Its plus is really a penalty to armor class.
  • Presence: gives the wearer a dignified, commanding air. For all encounter reactions he counts as having charisma 18. Friendly troops within 12" get +10% morale. The armor is very distinctive and works only when seen, so the wearer can't hope to blend into a crowd.
  • Blending: looks like normal armor, and detect magic doesn't reveal the property. At the command word it looks like ordinary clothes to everyone, while still working normally. Only true seeing shows what it really is.
  • Fear: looks like normal armor; detect magic shows only that it is magical. At the command word, the wearer gives off a fear aura in a 30-foot radius: every creature in it saves versus spell or flees in panic for one turn. The wearer is immune. Each use costs a charge. When the charges run out it is normal +1 armor, and it can't be recharged. The book prints two charge counts in the same paragraph: "2d4 fear charges when found" and "2d10 charges when found".
  • Possession: seems normal magic armor, with the plus from Table 76. But its maker put more than effort into it: the armor took in his personality and life force. The first time it is put on, and once a day after, the DM secretly rolls a save versus spell for the wearer. On a failure the life force begins to possess him. This is gradual, taking 3d4 days: first a few odd habits and possessiveness about the armor, then he drifts from old friends and haunts, wanders the streets looking for places the armorer knew, and has memories that aren't his. He refuses to take the armor off. At the end he is wholly possessed: he doesn't know his old friends or his own past, perhaps not even his class abilities, and may take a new name, a new alignment or a new class's abilities. If not freed, he becomes a non-player character under the DM's control. An exorcism spell breaks the possession and destroys the armor's personality. Dispel magic frees him long enough to take the armor off, but doesn't remove traits he has already absorbed. If the possessing influence is destroyed, the armor loses all its magic.
  • Healing: seems normal magic armor, but once a day, without warning and at no set time, it heals the wearer 2d6 points, wanted or not. Each healing uses a charge; it has 3d10 charges when found. When they run out it is +1 armor.

Weapons of quality

These aren't magical, just exceptionally well made. A character with the weaponsmith or bowyer proficiency can make them (see the proficiency).

  • Swords and miscellaneous melee weapons: forged of the finest steel, honed razor sharp, of the finest woods and so on. +1 to hit only. Worth 2d6 times the normal price.
  • Bows, crossbows and slings: perfectly balanced for pull and weight. Each range counts as the next shorter one for to-hit modifiers: short and medium both count as short, and long counts as medium. Beautifully made, worth 2d4 times the normal price.
  • Missile weapons: balanced to fly true and strike hard. +1 to hit only. Some are fancifully and tastefully decorated. Worth 2-5 times the normal price.
  • Martial arts weapons: made by martial arts masters who understand what the style demands. +1 to hit only, for someone trained in a martial arts style. Usually plain and simple looking; those who know martial arts will pay 2-5 times the normal price.
  • Ninja weapons: made with the ninja in mind. Ordinary looking, but razor sharp and finely balanced: +1 damage. Very light and compact; large ones come apart into small, easily hidden pieces and go back together in one round.

Magic properties

  • +1, +2, +3: the bonus applies to both to-hit and damage.
  • +1, +2, +3 damage: extra damage only, no bonus to hit.
  • +1, +2, +3 to hit: bonus to hit only, no extra damage.
  • +1, +2 vs. S: +1 to hit and damage against man-sized and larger creatures, +2 against smaller ones.
  • +1, +2 vs. L: +1 to hit and damage against man-sized and smaller creatures, +2 against larger ones.
  • -1, cursed: can't be told from a normal +1 weapon until used in earnest combat. A cursed bow is -1 to hit, and on a to-hit roll of 1 the missile comes back full force on the archer, for normal damage. A cursed melee weapon is -1 to hit; once picked up and used, the owner prefers it to all others and never willingly discards or ignores it. Remove curse frees him.
  • Accuracy +3: +3 to hit and damage, and every range counts as short (no range modifier).
  • Balance: seems a normal +1 weapon and is +1 to hit and damage. Carried, it gives exceptional balance: ninja get +10% to tightrope walking, and wherever balance matters (teetering on the edge of a pit and so on) the character automatically gets a save versus death to regain his footing, the weapon shifting or tugging him the fraction of an inch he needs. On a failed save he suffers the normal result.
  • Dancing: seems a +2 weapon and is +2 to hit and damage in hand. At the command word the martial arts weapon leaps to life and fights through the forms of the character's style, with as many attacks as his style gives and his chance to hit. He must have fought with it in the round before he speaks the word. It stays within five feet of him, fights for 2-5 rounds, then returns to his hands. The word works once a turn. It does nothing unless he knows a martial arts style that teaches this weapon.
  • Detection: +1 to hit and damage, and detects one kind of thing (roll 1d8: 1 evil, 10' radius; 2 good, 10' radius; 3 poison, by touch; 4 life forms, 10' radius; 5 back attacks, 1' range; 6 invisible creatures and objects, 10' radius; 7 traps, 5' radius; 8 secret doors, 10' radius). The character must hold it and speak the command word; if the answer is yes, the weapon tugs gently toward what it found.
  • Disruption: works exactly as the DMG's mace of disruption.
  • Distance +1: +1 to hit and damage, and every range category doubles.
  • Flame: +1 to hit and damage. At the command word it bursts into magic flame: +2d4 damage on a hit, sets combustibles alight 40% of the time, and sheds light in a 15-foot radius. It burns until the word is spoken again, and never harms the weapon, whatever it is made of.
  • Intelligence: +3 to hit and damage, with intelligence and powers as an intelligent sword, but never communicating beyond semi-empathy. Intelligence is 12-17 (1d6+11). Use the DMG's intelligent sword rules for its powers.
  • Silence: +1 to hit and damage. Held, it wraps the character in a muffling field that deadens (but doesn't stop) the sound he makes, while he still hears normally. A ninja gets +15% to move silently and +20% to hide in shadows. Sound-based attacks do half or no damage. The field covers only him and what he carries: something he drops or knocks over makes its normal noise. This property is explained in the book but isn't on Table 79.
  • Slaying: a +3 weapon marked or made in a distinctive way, easy to pick out from similar weapons. The markings show what kind of creature it slays. On a hit against that kind of creature, the creature dies at once, and the missile then loses all its magic. Possible creatures include bajang, bushi, dragons, elementals, giants, hengeyokai, hu hsien, humans, kalau, korobokuru, kuei, nats, ninja, ogre magi, ogres, oni, p'oh, samurai, shukenja, sohei, spiders, spirit folk, wu jen and yakuza; the DM can add to, change or limit the list to suit his campaign.
  • Speed: +1 to hit and damage. A speed bow (bow, crossbow or pellet bow) fires at double the normal rate and nocks or cocks itself, so the user automatically fires one shot first in the round. If surprised he can't react in time, though under complete surprise he can fire one shot in the second segment. A speed throwing weapon leaps from the hand: at the start of any round he holds it, he attacks first if he throws it. A speed martial arts weapon doubles the attacks his style allows with it, if he knows a style that teaches the weapon.
  • Unbreakable: counts as +2 to hit and damage. The weapon breaker special maneuver can't break it, and a foe who tries has a 75% chance of breaking his own weapon instead.

The wild lands between the Eastern Lands and the rest of the world have bred different ways of war, not just different ways of talking, eating and dressing.

The gajin knight sits on a heavy charger, cased in plate and mail with angled plates to turn crossbow bolts, peering through the slits of a visored helm. He carries a big shield, a lance 18 feet long or more, a heavy double-edged sword that relies on weight to cut through armor, and a flanged mace to batter and stun. His horse is bred big to carry iron barding and crash through footmen. His men-at-arms wear mail from head to toe and carry body shields, swords, spears, pikes, and mallets and axes to bring down knights on foot.

The samurai also rides to battle, but in a laced helmet with a great flaring neck guard, a sculpted metal face mask, a painted leather breastplate, broad plates over his upper arms and legs, and metal greaves. In his belt are two single-edged, pointed swords, one long and one short, for slashing and parrying with sharpness and speed. He carries a great lacquered bow he shoots from the saddle, a short naginata to slash at foes as he rides through their lines, and a quiver box of arrows: leaf heads, spikes, blunt heads, and perhaps a whistling arrow or two. His horse is bred for hardiness and speed, not mass. His men-at-arms are lightly armored, arms and legs bare, in iron hats instead of helms, with long naginatas and swords. The whole army is a mass of color: banners on the riders' backs, silk under armor, bright rows of lacing.

The knight relies on the might of his weapons and armor; the samurai on speed and sharpness. He doesn't batter a foe down but cuts him down quickly, and though he can charge, he prefers to shoot from horseback. Peasants differ too: the gajin yeoman defends his land with an old sword and farm tools made into weapons, while the peasant of the Eastern Lands, often forbidden weapons, has learned to fight with his hands and feet and a range of small, unusual tools.

OA uses the normal 1eFRPG rules for combat, with the additions below for these styles and techniques.

The combat round, with the OA additions

  1. Surprise: each side checks; characters are normally surprised on 1-2 on 1d6. Sometimes surprise isn't possible because of visibility, surroundings, noise and so on. OA: iaijutsu can change the roll (below).
  2. Declare actions: players say what their characters will try. OA: they must also say if a character is trying to subdue, disarm or unhorse an opponent.
  3. Initiative: if no one is surprised, each side rolls 1d6; the higher roll goes first this round. OA: kensai and wu jen can modify the roll (below).
  4. The winning side acts: OA: first, any kensai or wu jen whose modified roll beats both sides acts. Then each character on the winning side rolls 1d20 to hit, compared to the target's armor class on his class's combat table; equal or higher, with strength, magic and other modifiers, is a hit. OA: some characters must say whether they are using ki power before rolling. Targets of spells make their saving throws. OA: a shukenja must say whether he is using ki power before any saving throw is made. Roll damage for each hit, adding strength, magic weapons, weapons of quality and ki powers, and subtract it from the target's hit points. OA: subdual damage isn't subtracted but noted separately.
  5. The losing side acts as in step 4.

Surprise and iaijutsu

A character with the iaijutsu proficiency draws his weapon with lightning speed, which can catch others by surprise, but only in special situations: when a peaceful encounter suddenly turns violent. Picture a player character and a non-player character kneeling side by side in heated negotiations, swords sheathed. Tension rises, and the non-player character suddenly draws and lunges. Surprise is rolled to see who is ready, and how fast each can draw is everything.

  • If one has iaijutsu and the other doesn't, the one without it has -1 on his surprise roll.
  • If both have it, both have -1.
  • There is no modifier when weapons are already drawn, or the opponent has reason to expect an attack. It applies only when a peaceful situation erupts into bloodshed, especially from an unexpected quarter.

Initiative modifiers

Each round, unless someone is surprised, 1d6 is rolled for initiative, normally unmodified. But people of the Eastern Lands live by their quickness, and some have trained their speed until they are more likely to strike the first, crucial blow.

  • Each side still rolls once. A character with a modifier applies it to his side's roll for his own actions only, so a round may split into more than two phases of attacks.
  • Ties aren't rerolled: everyone tied acts at the same instant. Damage and spell effects against a character acting at the same moment don't take effect until he finishes his own action; then he suffers them normally.
  • If one side's roll beats even the highest modified roll on the other side, the whole winning side acts in any order it likes, all before the other side.

Example: a 1st level kensai, samurai and shukenja meet a band of hostile samurai. The player characters roll 3; the non-player characters roll 4. The kensai (modified to 4) and the non-player characters strike first, at the same instant, then the samurai and shukenja. Had the other band included a kensai, he would have struck first (on 5), then the rest of his band and the player character kensai together, then the surviving player characters.

text.content:
Source: OA p.99-101 (Missile Fire from Horseback; Unhorsing; Disarming; Subduing Opponents; The Psychic Duel; Table 67). Rewritten in plain words. Table 67 was checked against the page image.

Shooting from horseback

The mounted archer is central to the armies of the Eastern Lands. Hordes of riders on swift ponies sweep across the plains, shooting from the saddle; warriors practice until they can hit targets at full gallop with great bows. It is no show: horse archers gallop at the enemy, loose their arrows, wheel away out of reach of foot archers, and raid camps without stopping. On the rare occasions gajin armies marched against them, disaster was the usual result: their slogging ranks were thinned by arrows, the riders galloped off before the footmen could shoot back, and knights who charged were simply avoided and shot down.

  • Anyone can shoot from a horse that is standing still.
  • Shooting from a moving horse takes the horsemanship proficiency, since a bow needs both hands and the rider must guide the horse with his knees. The DM can rule that very rough ground (rocky slopes, thick brush and so on) needs the reins, which stops shooting.
  • Rate of fire from horseback is half normal: 2/1 becomes 1/1, 3/1 becomes 3/2, and so on.
  • The rider has a penalty to hit for the horse's speed (Table 67), added to the modifiers for range, weapon against armor type and so on.
  • In a round he shoots, the horse can only turn slightly, at most 30 degrees either way. Sharper turns or maneuvers stop him shooting.
  • The same rules apply on any horse-like creature that horsemanship covers.
