OA Table 67: Horseback Bowfire Modifiers.

Unhorsing

Where horsemen are so formidable, footmen want them off their horses, where they can be outnumbered and overpowered.

  • Killing the horse puts the rider on foot at once, by missile or melee. But horses are valuable, and often the prize the attackers want, so this is a last resort.
  • Struck by a rider: when a rider is hit by a melee weapon 3 feet or longer, wielded by another mounted character, on a natural 20, he may fall. Without horsemanship he falls, taking an extra 1d3 damage. With it, he rolls against the proficiency: success keeps him in the saddle (he still takes the hit's damage); failure means he falls as above.
  • Struck by a footman: a footman with a melee weapon 5 to 9 feet long has the same chance as a rider. One with a weapon 10 feet or longer unhorses on 16-20 on 1d20 (25%). Either way the rider gets his horsemanship roll to stay on.
  • Diving from the saddle: a rider can pull alongside another and leap at him. A hit means he has grabbed him; a miss means he falls to the ground. The grabbed rider rolls against horsemanship: on a failure both fall, taking 1d6 each; on a success he stays in the saddle with the attacker hanging off his side. The attacker must hit again every turn to force another proficiency roll; if he misses, he falls (and takes damage). Meanwhile the rider can strike at him at -2 to hit.
  • Pulled down by footmen: only man-sized or larger creatures can try; larger ones count as two men. The footman must grab the rider as he passes with a to-hit roll at -2 if the horse moves 6" or less, -4 at 7" to 12", or -6 faster than 12". If he hits, the rider rolls against horsemanship to stay on. If the attempt fails and the horse is moving faster than 12", the horse gets a free set of attacks on the footman. Each extra footman grabbing (up to 4) gives -1 to the rider's roll. A rider pulled down by more than one man takes no damage, since he likely lands on someone. Eight men around a horse can pull down horse and rider together. Horse and rider attack normally throughout.
  • Prepared defenses: given time and materials, ropes strung between trees at rider height, tripwires and similar tricks can unhorse riders; the DM decides how well they work. Sharpened stakes stop charges: two men can stake a 10-foot square in an hour with stakes 4 to 5 feet long, if bamboo or light wood is at hand. Stakes are easy to see and avoid by turning aside, or a rider can urge his horse through, which takes a proficiency roll as for a jump or leap. A horse that enters the stakes hits 1d4-1 (0-3) stakes per 10 feet of depth, one fewer with chain barding and two fewer with plate, each doing 2d6 damage to the horse.
  • These rules work for any ridden creature.

Disarming

Sometimes characters need to disarm a foe: a charmed friend attacking them, or someone they want to capture without getting badly hurt.

  • With a weapon: the character needs a melee weapon at least as big as the victim's, and must say at the start of the round that he is disarming. He rolls to hit normally but does no damage; instead the victim saves versus petrification or drops the weapon, which lands 1d6 feet away. Picking it up takes a round.
  • Bare-handed: use the weaponless combat rules in the UA, or martial arts if the character has it. With martial arts he can knock loose a weapon of any size, the same way as with a weapon, but the victim gets +2 on his save.
  • Two-handed weapons: a success knocks loose only one hand, so two successes in the same round are needed. With only one, the foe simply regrips at the end of the round.

Subduing

Sometimes the goal is to beat an opponent without killing him: shukenja are normally forbidden to kill, and prisoners and hostages are only useful alive.

  • Only creatures of at least low intelligence can be subdued. Those of genius intelligence or higher are subdued only if they choose to surrender; they know what happens to most prisoners. Any creature or non-player character can be subdued, but a player character can never be forced to submit; surrendering is the player's choice.
  • Subduing must be declared at the start of the fight. Attackers then strike with the back, flat, haft, butt, pommel or hilt. Roll damage normally: 1/4 is lost from hit points, and 3/4 is subdual damage, recorded separately.
  • When subdual damage passes the creature's full (not current) hit points, it is subdued and surrenders. If anyone attacks it for normal damage after subduing was declared, it won't surrender: all subdual damage vanishes and it is fought normally.
  • A subdued creature stops fighting and drops its weapons. If the characters can talk with it, they can demand an oath: a task or promise such as "Leave this province never to return", "Go to your lord and tell him of your humiliating defeat", or "Swear never to haunt this place again". The DM secretly rolls against its honor (if it has honor points) or makes it save versus death. If the roll is equal to or under its honor, or it fails the save, it obeys. Otherwise it pretends to agree and plans revenge.
  • Instead, the victor can keep it captive. It escapes at the first chance, staying meek only while its captors keep the upper hand.

The psychic duel

Two fierce samurai face off in a dusty street. Neither moves; only flies buzz; sweat runs down their mustaches. Then one bobs his head in a bow, turns, and slips away into the crowd. The other grins: he has won without touching his sword.

That is a psychic duel: a hidden struggle of will, courage, skill and determination between proud warriors. Any race or class can try it; it isn't psionic. It shows in a faint grimace, a flicker of an eyelid, a twitching muscle. Will he attack with wild abandon? Is he calm and sure of his skill? Will he risk certain death? A character who shows such qualities may win without a fight, and the wise man knows when he is outmatched and yields before it comes to blows.

  • When: only between intelligent humans or humanoids, one against one. Never between friends or companions, which dishonors both (-3 honor each). Not if they have already crossed weapons in this encounter, and not if others attack them during it. So not in the heat of battle, but perhaps as a challenge before it, or to put a swaggering bully in his place.
  • How: both spend the round within 10 feet of each other, focusing their will, then each saves versus death. Kensai get +2 against non-kensai. One success and one failure: the one who succeeded wins. Both fail: no one wins. Both succeed: they stay locked together for another round. Anyone who breaks off and attacks before it is settled loses; his nerve broke.
  • Winning: +2 honor if the loser is of higher level, +1 if the same level, nothing if lower.
  • Losing: the loser either retreats, losing as much honor as the winner gained, or attacks anyway. If he attacks, he is -1 on initiative, to-hit and saving throw rolls for the whole fight. There is no surprise roll, since both are ready.

Source: OA p.101-102 and 105-106 (Martial Arts; Styles; Stunning and Incapacitating; Learning Martial Arts; Multiple Styles and Combining Styles; Table 68). Rewritten in plain words. Table 68 was checked against the page image.

Martial arts never developed far in the rest of the world. In the Eastern Lands the body itself becomes a weapon that can beat foes who seem better armed and armored: hands, feet, legs, arms, head, any part. It takes rigorous training and great physical and mental discipline to master the styles, maneuvers and feats: to anticipate, harden the body, shut out pain, and call up energy from deep within. It demands real commitment.

Why here:

  • Philosophy: people throughout these lands believe in the forces of nature, not as ideas but as energies charging everything around them. A person is part of those forces and can draw on them, and strives to live in harmony with them, through offerings, prayers or understanding. First he must master and harmonize the forces within himself. Tools change nature but stand outside that harmony, so knowing one's own body leads to fighting without weapons.
  • Religion: several faiths teach that the world is passing and possessions have no lasting worth, only a person's inner qualities. Relying on a weapon is relying on the material world, so devout followers develop their own abilities instead.
  • Law: where a gajin peasant feels entitled to carry a sword, lords here often pass harsh edicts against owning weapons, especially in conquered or troublesome provinces, with punishments up to torture and execution. Commoners found other ways to defend themselves.

In time these skills became widespread and honorable. Styles and training were made regular, studied scientifically and religiously, until unarmed fighting became an art that, practiced rightly, leads the student toward self-perfection. Every land developed its own styles, to counter local weapons and copy local beasts, and every master developed his own moves, so two masters of one style may fight quite differently. Arguments over which style was best were common, and challenges between schools drew hundreds of onlookers.

At root, martial arts teach a fighter to avoid being hurt. Some styles do this defensively, turning aside or dodging; some aggressively, holding that attack is the best defense; some by mastering many weapons. Techniques include punches, blocks, kicks, pushes, throws, holds, locks and dodges. "Unarmed" is a misnomer: students often learn common and unusual weapons, which take the same discipline as the open-hand forms and are taught only as part of a style. A peasant handed a tui-fa is no threat; a master with one is deadly.

These rules don't list every move of a style. A style is defined by its effects in play: attacks, damage, armor class and principal attack form. As characters rise in level they may learn the special maneuvers of their style, but only with dedication and training.

Styles

A style has five features: number of attacks, damage, armor class, principal attack form and special maneuvers. Every combination is a different style, learned separately. Styles often have descriptive or poetic names: animals (Snake, Monkey, Tiger), poetry (Eight Drunken Fairies), or descriptions (Empty Hand, Springing Legs, Eight Fists). Some are highly defensive and rely on inner power; others are aggressive, with hard, sudden attacks.

  • Number of attacks works as in normal combat, but depends on the style, so a character may attack more, fewer or the same number of times as with weapons. It applies only when fighting in that style.
  • Damage is the die rolled on a hit. Defensive styles usually do little; offensive ones more.
  • Armor class is the protection the training gives, by avoiding, turning or withstanding blows.
  • Principal attack form is the body part the style uses most. As long as it is free, the character can attack effectively: a karate fighter, who uses his fists, can still attack with his legs held.
  • Special maneuvers are the secrets of the art: fantastic feats such as backward kick, sticking touch, great throw and ironskin, hard to learn (see Creating a Style).

Some styles list maneuvers above difficulty 1 without the easier ones of that method (Kung-fu's Kick 2, for example); the progression rule counts across all methods, so these are as printed. Each style is also an item in the OA Martial Arts compendium.

Stunning and incapacitating

Every style can stun or incapacitate a man-sized foe. On an unmodified 20 to hit, the victim saves versus paralyzation. If he saves, he just takes normal damage. If he fails, compare the number rolled on his save to his hit dice or level: if it is lower, he is stunned for 1d6 rounds; if higher, he is out for 1-3 hours. Creatures with +4 or more on their hit dice count as one die higher.

Example: a martial artist rolls 20 against a lizard man, which fails its save with a 2. That equals the lizard man's 2+1 hit dice, so it is stunned for 1d6 rounds. Had it rolled 6, it would have been out for 1-3 hours. (The book doesn't say what happens when the roll exactly equals the hit dice except through this example, which treats it as stunned.)

Learning martial arts

A martial arts style costs a proficiency slot like any other proficiency, but it is harder to learn and has extra requirements.

Finding a master. "Master" is an honorary title, not a class, and says nothing of skill or level. A master might be a peasant, a hermit developing his own style, a traveling bushi, a teacher with a school in a town, a famous samurai, or a temple priest teaching his followers. Some masters are brilliant and famous, some skilled, some barely able to teach the basics, and some incompetent behind an impressive title; students find out as they study.

  • Masters can be hard to find. Many guard their art as a secret for a chosen few (many styles have died with their masters), don't display their skill because it would be proud and boastful (and might anger the gods), or hope never to have to use it. Some believe their art can be learned only in tranquil seclusion deep in the mountains.
  • Politics hides them too: conquered peoples may be forbidden their arts, and nervous emperors, warlords or daimyos may destroy powerful temples, the usual centers of training, scattering masters and students into secret societies.
  • Still, towns and cities may have schools run by well-known masters that students travel far to reach. Characters will hear of such schools, and sometimes of the secretive masters.

Being accepted.

  • A character with no martial arts presents himself humbly and respectfully, with a 10% chance of being accepted at once. Usually he is politely sent away. He then courts the master, returning with small gifts; each visit that pleases the master (and stays respectful) adds 10% to the chance. He can keep returning until accepted, or until he offends the master, who will then never take him.
  • A character who already knows some martial arts can challenge the master, which is always accepted. The master decides whether he or a student fights; if the challenger isn't well known, a student is assigned, which is customary and no insult. Challenges are fought to subdue (usually preferred, sparing needless killing) or to the death; a death in a challenge isn't a crime and the victor is rarely punished. Crowds may gather to watch. If the challenger wins, the master accepts him (and may hope to learn from him). If he loses, he can leave and return when more skilled, or humbly beg to be accepted, which works especially well after a humiliating defeat.

What the master knows. The master always knows the basics (armor class, attacks, damage). For weapons, the DM counts the style's weapons and rolls the smallest die equal to or above that number: the result is how many he knows. He does the same for the style's special maneuvers. The master knows maneuvers from the easiest up, under the same rule as students, and never learns more unless the DM rules otherwise.

Training.

  • After at least a month with the master, the character spends one slot and gains the basics: armor class, number of attacks and damage, but no special maneuvers or weapons.
  • He is then free to travel and adventure, but must practice at least an hour a day and spend six hours a week with his master; otherwise he can't add maneuvers or weapons.
  • Each further slot adds one special maneuver or weapon of the style. He doesn't suddenly know it; he is assumed to have been practicing. No more than two slots can be spent on one style per level.
  • Maneuvers must be learned in order of difficulty: all difficulty 1 maneuvers before any difficulty 2, and so on.
  • Once he has learned all the master knows, he can seek another master who knows more, or teaches another style.

More than one style

  • A character can learn several styles, with a master for each, enough slots and enough dedication.
  • In a fight he chooses one style and has only its abilities and maneuvers, except maneuvers that are always in effect. He can change style from round to round.
  • Once he has two or more styles and has learned all their masters know, he can create his own style, mixing their elements as he likes (one style's armor class with another's attacks and damage, say) and combining all the maneuvers he knows. He can teach it as a master.

Source: OA p.102-103 (Creating a Style; Notes Regarding Style Combination Table; Special Maneuvers; Tables 69 and 70). Rewritten in plain words. Tables 69 and 70 were checked against the page images.

The DM is encouraged to create new styles for his campaign, taught by non-player character masters. You never know when a hermit in the hills has developed a new fighting style.

1. Form: hard, soft or both

  • Hard styles use muscle and bone for power, with direct movements, and are generally offensive.
  • Soft styles draw on inner power (though they still condition the muscles), with fluid, circular movements, and are generally defensive: they turn the attacker's force against him and strike only once he has committed himself. Training is more mental, teaching the student to focus his inner power.
  • Hard/soft styles combine both: gentle circular defense with swift direct attacks, physical training balanced with mental.
  • Any style can use a number of unusual weapons.

2. Principal method

The principal method is how the style most often attacks: kicking styles kick a lot, throwing styles rely on grappling and leverage, and so on. Every style also uses moves from other methods, since relying on one would mean certain defeat.

3. Work out the style

  • Pick one form and one principal method.
  • Armor class: add the two AC mods and subtract the total from 10.
  • Attacks: add the two attacks mods; that is the attacks per round in this style only, not in any other style or with normal weapons.
  • Damage: add the two damage mods and round up to the nearest die used in the game: 4 is 1d4, 5 or 6 is 1d6.
  • Body part: the method's body part. As long as it is free, the character can attack effectively in the style. (Throwing uses the whole body.)
  • Weapons: roll 1d4 and subtract 2 for how many weapons the style teaches, chosen from the weapons usable only with martial arts.

4. Special maneuvers

Special maneuvers take intensive study but give better-than-normal results. Some are actions tried during a fight (flying kick, one finger); some, once learned, are always in effect (ironskin, blind fighting).

  • A combat maneuver costs one or more of the character's attacks that round, and is risky: failure often leaves him exposed.
  • A movement maneuver counts as movement, so he makes no attacks that round unless the maneuver says otherwise.
  • Maneuvers are grouped by principal method and marked hard, soft or hard/soft, matching the style's form. Soft styles mostly use soft maneuvers and hard styles hard ones, but they can cross over.
  • Mental and Physical Training maneuvers can be learned in any style, through its practice and discipline.

Choosing the style's maneuvers:

  • Roll 1d8: that many maneuvers come from the style's principal method or from Mental and Physical Training.
  • Then roll 1-3 more from other methods (or Mental and Physical Training again). Most styles borrow a few to round out their tactics.
  • The number by each maneuver is its difficulty; lower is easier. The style's maneuvers must run upward from 1, but the run can cross methods and include several of the same difficulty. For example: circle kick (1), flying kick (2), all-around sight (2), backward kick (3). A character learns them in that order; he can learn a harder one only once the easier ones are learned.
  • Maneuvers aren't gained when the style is first learned; see Learning Martial Arts on the Martial Arts page.

Source: OA p.107-109 (Events and Encounters; The Calendar; Yearly Events; Monthly Events, with the example year). Rewritten in plain words. The calendar and Tables 71-73 were checked against the page images.

The Eastern Lands are rich and varied, full of wondrous palaces, crumbling shrines and stout castles, where things happen from the exotic to the everyday. They also change: people die and children are born, earthquakes shatter villages and new homes go up, nations conquer neighbors and rebellions are crushed. These events, and the changes they bring, are part of the characters' daily lives.

Four kinds of event

  • Yearly (major) events sweep across whole provinces or empires: a great earthquake is more than a few characters can stop (though they can try, and rarely succeed). They seldom involve the characters directly, but can't be ignored: fallen buildings and moved rivers change what the characters know and perhaps what they own. They are rare, at most one a year, but their shock is profound.
  • Monthly (secondary) events happen less often than daily ones but affect the characters more. When bandits set up in the characters' home province, caravans need guards and rewards go up for the villains' heads. At most one a month, or life would get too exciting.
  • Daily events happen on the road and at home. Often they are trivial; sometimes they bring information, ideas, help or clues; often they lead to action: bandits fall on the camp, a man-eating tiger stalks the forest. Check daily, or several times a day in dangerous areas.
  • Hourly events: in places the characters search slowly and carefully, such as a ninja village or a haunted temple ruin, things happen fast. Check several times an hour.

The DM works out the yearly and monthly events at the start of play and at the start of each game year. Knowing them in advance lets him prepare (new maps after a great earthquake), plant the build-up (the armies and the rumors of war), put the characters in the right place at the right time (as soldiers or commanders in the coming war, or courtiers of a prince about to be assassinated), and answer fate, divination and similar spells with confidence.

The calendar

Long ago, a great emperor of Shou Lung set a calendar to fix the regular holidays and festivals. It has been so successful that it is used throughout the civilized Eastern Lands. The year begins sometime in our February or March.

  • Festivals are celebrations lasting several days, even weeks.
  • Feasts are reasons to gather for as lavish a banquet as people can afford.
  • Holy days may or may not be kept, depending on the local religion and people. Observances are simple, often an excuse for a feast.

Rolling the year

  1. Yearly event first, on "OA Table 71: Yearly Events" in the OA Tables compendium. There is only one a year, it holds for the whole year, and it often decides which monthly events happen. Roll only for the campaign area (Kozakura alone, if the characters are there), unless the characters will travel widely or there are groups in several places; then roll for every land they are involved in (Kozakura and Shou Lung, if they start in one and go to the other).
  2. Month: roll 1d12 for the month the event happens or begins. Some events, such as an earthquake, are over quickly; a war can last a whole campaign season. Each description gives how long it lasts.
  3. Monthly events: roll one for each month on Table 72, using the column that fits that month. The OA Tables compendium has each column as its own roll table: "OA Table 72: Monthly Events: Assassination, Incursion, Political Plot, Rebellion, War" for months of armed violence or its threat; "...: Natural Disaster" for months of floods, typhoons, droughts, famines, plagues and their aftermath (as the event description says); and "...: Other" when all is well. Note each event beside its month. The DM can change any event that doesn't fit the year, and should add his own: the lists are only a small selection.
  4. Story: read each description and build a story that ties the year together.

Example year in T'u Lung. The DM rolls 82 for the yearly event: Rebellion. 1d12 gives 5, so a province rises in Kao II; the DM decides the plotters will strike during the Dragon Boat Festival, hoping to catch the government off guard. Rebellion lasts 1d6 months; he rolls 3 and decides the government wins in the end. The first four months use the "other" column, the next three the armed violence column, and the rest the "other" column again:

1. Tsou: Famous Person2. Ju: VIP Visit3. Yu: Bandit Activity
4. Kao: Bandit Activity5. Kao II: Rebellion; Incursion, Minor6. Chu: Bandit Activity
7. Hsiang: Recruiting8. Chuang: Injustice9. Hsuan: Accident
10. Yang: Haunting11. Ku: Bandit Activity12. Tu: Marriage

The story: early in the year, a powerful wizard who leads a secret society visits the province, and the society lays its plans. Then an imperial censor (a powerful official, something like secret police) calls on the ruler to check reports of unrest, but learns little. For the next two months, bandits in the mountains grow bolder; they are really society members testing the province's soldiers. In Kao II they are joined by troops from a neighboring warlord, and together they rouse unhappy peasants and rogues to revolt. They do well at first, then suffer setbacks. In Chu the rebels fall back to the mountains and raid. At last the government conscripts every able-bodied man it can find and drives them out of their strongholds; the rebellion is broken, though many escape. Reprisals follow: whole families of suspected helpers are executed, jailed or banished, and many people use the chance to settle old scores or steal property, so many innocents are accused. In Hsuan a bridge collapses and several people fall to their deaths; the next month rumor says the rebuilt bridge is haunted by them, and it can't be finished until that is dealt with. In Ku, bandits return to the hills, backed by the same warlord. Finally the governor arranges a marriage between one of his daughters and one of the warlord's sons, and the year ends with great celebration and feasting.

A year like this gives characters of every level something to do. High-level characters may be caught up in the rebels' intrigue and the censor's visit, or command the forces against the rebellion (or join it). Mid-level characters may be rebels, the censor's secret helpers, officers of smaller government units, overseers of the bridge rebuilding, or envoys arranging the marriage. Low-level characters may guard a caravan the bandits attack, spy for the rebels, be pressed into government service, or be there when the bridge falls.

The characters can change things. The year's events don't account for what the characters do, and they (especially high-level ones) may change many outcomes: find enough evidence for the censor to stop the rebellion, lead it to victory, stop the cruelty after it, or wreck the governor's marriage plans. When they do, the DM should change the rest of the year to match, deciding the new events himself when they are obvious or rerolling them. The yearly event is never rerolled: if the characters prevent it, there is no yearly event that year.

Source: OA p.109-110 (Explanation of Yearly Events; Table 71). Rewritten in plain words; numbers checked against the page images.

Roll on "OA Table 71: Yearly Events" in the OA Tables compendium. For large battles the book recommends a separate mass-combat rules supplement; without one, use the durations given here.

  • Ambassador: an ambassador arrives from another land (50%) or is sent to one (50%), and stays 3d10 months. Ambassadors come to prevent war, make an alliance, arrange a marriage, pay tribute, promote trade or gain culture. An arrival is a major event at court, with ceremonies and banquets. 10% of arriving ambassadors are gajin from the distant lands beyond the Eastern Lands.
  • Assassination of a lord: a high-ranking lord (emperor, prince, chieftain, daimyo, governor, prime minister or minister of state) is assassinated. Characters who are his vassals or have dealt with him may fall under suspicion; known enemies are suspected automatically. 30% chance the assassin is taken alive, and 1% that he accuses the characters (if they have any tie to the victim). 20% chance there is no clear heir, and a power struggle lasts 1d6 months (perhaps war, if the DM likes). Otherwise the court is in turmoil for 1d6 months, then returns to normal.
  • Birth: a child is born to a high-ranking noble family, securing the line. The noble and those under him celebrate with feasts and ceremonies for several days.
  • Comet: a bright comet is seen for 1d4 weeks, an omen of some great event. The DM chooses a second yearly event, which happens soon after the comet passes.
  • Death of a lord: a high-ranking noble dies, in battle, by misadventure, of disease, or peacefully in bed. Succession works as for an assassination.
  • Earthquake, major: a powerful quake causes great destruction within a 50-mile radius of a center the DM chooses. Lesser tremors before and after do slight damage (DM's choice). The great quake destroys cities, reshapes lakes, coasts and rivers, starts great fires and may kill hundreds. Characters and their property in the radius are affected as by an earthquake spell (severity chosen by the DM). 70% chance of a major fire in any town or city, and 40% of a plague in any populated area. The quake lasts only a few hours.
  • Famine: drought and poor harvests bring famine, with obvious warning signs: crops wither, animals die, the poor go hungry. It lasts 2-7 months. Food costs 10, 50 or even 100 times normal. Marauding bands appear, taking any food they can find: cattle, sheep, dogs, horses. Farms earn nothing this year and 25% of normal next year. 60% chance of a peasant uprising unless the suffering is relieved. Population falls 5% per month of famine. 20% chance of plague.
  • Fire, major: a huge fire destroys 50% to 80% of a major city. The characters' property there burns down with a chance equal to the part of the city destroyed. The city loses 10% to 40% of its people. 20% chance of plague and 10% of famine. Lumber and building materials cost 10 times normal for four months, and food doubles for one month.
  • Flood: on a coast, storms flood the coastal lands; on a river, heavy rains send it over its banks onto the bottom lands. The water rises 5-30 feet (5d6). Warning signs show 2-5 days ahead, time to build levees and dikes. Once it starts, the water rises 1/2 foot an hour to its peak, stays there 4d6 hours, then falls 1 foot a day. Buildings are badly damaged, but only those in the path of the raging water are destroyed. Population falls 1% to 10%, and all goods cost double for 2-5 months. Normal movement across flooded land is impossible. A flood in planting season halves farm income for the year; one at harvest loses 80% of farm income, with a 40% chance of famine in 1-3 months unless steps are taken. Every flood has a 20% chance of plague. Floods don't happen in deserts or dry lands.
  • Incursion, major: a great migration of creatures enters the kingdom from outside. It isn't war, but isn't necessarily peaceful. Its size suits the kingdom's: several hundred for a small province, several thousand for a large kingdom. The newcomers may be humans, humanoids or monsters (a barbarian horde driven from its homeland, or hobgoblins spreading out). They keep their old ways and language, and keep raiding if that is their habit. They stay until driven out; if allowed to stay, over the years they take on local ways until they are an ordinary part of life. The migration takes 1d12 months.
  • Marriage: the ruler arranges an important diplomatic marriage for himself or a child, to secure an alliance, gain control of smaller kingdoms, settle a dispute or appease an overlord. Festivals and feasting follow.
  • New religion: a new religion, or a new sect of an old one, appears and quickly wins followers. 75% chance it leads to hostility and feuding with the established faiths: skirmishes, burned temples, battles between warrior monks. Both sides seek the ruler's support; 60% chance he favors the newcomers, and if so, 40% chance he bans the other religions, burning their temples, forbidding their practices and killing or banishing their priests. Rulers often back new religions to break the political power of old ones. The new faith takes 2-7 months to arrive; the feuding may last centuries.
  • Plague: a terrible disease spreads faster than priests can stop it with spells, lasting 2d6 months. Each month in the plague lands gives a 40% chance of catching it; being with a sick person, 60%. Population falls 5% a month. The healthy, and people in neighboring lands, distrust strangers. Traders stay away: imported goods cost five times normal and ordinary goods double. Unless the country is small, the plague doesn't strike everywhere at once but sweeps from town to town like a scythe, so a town may not have been hit yet, may be suffering now, or may already have survived it.
  • Political plot: a plot to overthrow the government is discovered, or the ruler becomes convinced there is one. Many nobles and officials are stripped of rank, banished or executed. Characters in government or politics have a 40% chance of being accused of taking part (80% if they have powerful enemies), and must prove their innocence or suffer the consequences. 20% chance a noble or group of nobles rebels. Spies and secret police are everywhere, ready to arrest on the slightest evidence. The turmoil lasts 1-3 months.
  • Rebellion: a powerful lord, secret society, religious sect, army commander or peasant army tries to overthrow the government in the area, for independence, to escape taxes and brutal treatment, for special privileges, or to seize the throne. The DM decides the cause, strength and outcome. If the characters fight in its battles, the book strongly recommends using mass-combat rules, and the DM can give the players command and strategy for either side, a whole series of adventures in itself. Without it, the rebellion lasts 1d6 months and then succeeds (highly unlikely) or fails. Captured rebels can expect no mercy.
  • Tsunami: a great wave strikes a 50-mile stretch of coast, with the same effects as the tsunami spell. It is 100 to 200 feet high when it hits, with little warning. Population there falls 70%. Countries with no coast have no event this year. 10% chance of plague afterward. Building materials cost triple and everything else double in the area for 1-2 months.
  • Visitation: a major deity appears somewhere in the land, for good or ill, and the news spreads fast. A revered site draws pilgrims, and the religion or sect builds a temple or shrine there. A despised site brings misfortune to everyone within 5 miles: common folk move away if they can, the area is shunned, and it becomes a secret meeting place for evil followers and monsters.
  • Volcano: a dormant volcano erupts (70%) or a new one appears (30%), after tremors and rumbles like those before a major earthquake. The eruption is extremely violent: everything within 5 miles is destroyed, and thick ash falls up to 30 miles downwind. It smokes and spews ash for the rest of the month, then stays active for 1d12 months, with a 10% chance each month of another major eruption.
  • War: the ruler attacks a neighboring land (50%) or is invaded by one (50%), with armies of thousands or tens of thousands. The DM decides the causes, forces and outcome. With mass-combat rules, he may give the characters commands in one of the armies. One major campaign is fought each year, lasting 2-5 months (usually in summer), and the war lasts 1-3 years. Characters are readily accepted into the army and may rise quickly. Prices along the campaign route double or triple, farm income in the fought-over land halves, and civilians usually move away. Away from the front, others may take the chance to rebel or rise up. Press gangs roam the countryside looking for "recruits", and younger sons of peasants leave home to seek fame and fortune as soldiers.

Source: OA p.110-112 (Explanation of Monthly Events; Table 72). Rewritten in plain words; numbers checked against the page images.

Roll on the column of "OA Table 72: Monthly Events" (three roll tables in the OA Tables compendium) that fits the month.

  • Accident: a terrible accident: a bridge over a raging river collapses, lightning strikes a building, a horse cart runs wild through the streets, a levee breaks. The DM decides what. At best it is an inconvenience, at worst a great loss of life, and people talk about it for a long time.
  • Bad harvest: bad weather, lazy farmers, bad luck and greedy crows make a poor crop. Farm income falls 25%. 5% chance of famine. Food costs 50% more. Peasants grow unhappy and grumble about ill luck and bad fate, and often blame the ruler, as if the poor harvest were punishment for his evil deeds.
  • Bad weather: the whole month's weather is foul: blizzards choke the roads in winter with freezing air; monsoon rains turn everything to a sodden mess; hot weather is exceptionally hot and miserable. All movement is halved, and trade with it. Armies in the field lose 15% to desertion as common soldiers decide they have had enough. In the growing season, crops are damaged: farm income falls 15%.
  • Bandit activity: 20-200 bandits move into the area and are very active, driven from a neighboring region or drawn here. They build a stronghold somewhere remote, preferably deep in the mountains, with spies and informers in the towns and villages watching for caravans and treasury shipments. Any caravan through the region has a base 50% chance of attack; lone travelers are robbed 80% of the time; a merchant or official foolish enough to say publicly that he carries valuable cargo is attacked automatically. Mercenary guards are in great demand. An effective government sends troops to drive them out (perhaps several battles suited to mass-combat rules). Merchants and travelers distrust strangers. If the government's troops fail, the bandits raid small villages, stealing their grain after each harvest, and stay until defeated or until the pickings get too slim.
  • Birth: a married character learns that he or she will have a child, born in nine months. If that doesn't apply, a local noble or official has a child (95%), or there are reports of a miraculous birth in a peasant family (5%). A noble's child brings feasting for the noble and his retainers. A miraculous birth is a wonder: the child springs from a cut bamboo stalk, appears from the waters of a spring, is found in a local shrine, and so on. The peasant family is always hard-working, honest and pious. As the child grows, he proves exceptional in some way (great strength, cleverness, magical ability), and the family's fortunes rise until they lead their community.
  • Death: a local noble or official dies of natural causes, war or misadventure.
    • A hereditary post goes to his son. If he has no heir, 30% chance someone else has inherited (by adoption or assignment of rights), and the succession goes smoothly.
    • If succession is unclear and the central government is strong, the court gives the fief to a new lord, with political maneuvering at court for it (fierce struggles for a rich farming province). If the central government is weak or absent, neighboring lords try to take the fief by force, which can mean fighting across the province.
    • For a government post, the central government sends a new official, who arrives in 2-7 weeks. Until then no business of that post can be settled: with the magistrate dead, no cases are heard until the new one comes.
  • Earthquake, minor: a minor quake strikes a 5-mile radius around a center the DM chooses, after tremors like those before a major quake. Little loss of life, but 50% of the buildings in the area are damaged. 20% chance of a major fire and 30% of a minor fire. Building materials cost double for 1-2 months.
  • Excessive taxes: the ruler sets peasants' taxes at an impossible rate, to pay for a campaign, rebuild after a disaster, or simply because he is corrupt and wasteful. Poorer peasants fall into poverty or debt slavery, and many sell their land and beg. Everyone seeks a way out, petitioning for exemptions or hiding goods. 30% chance of an uprising and 70% of more bandit activity as ruined peasants flee to the hills.
  • Famous person: a renowned person with no official post arrives, noted for exceptional skill in an art or craft: painting in the classical style, mastery of a difficult poetry form, superb fighting form, brilliant philosophy, or a name for piety. He may have a class and level like a player character, or be a non-player character with other skills. He tries to arrive quietly and keep out of notice, but rumors of him and his fame soon spread. He may have secret reasons for being there; the DM adds whatever complications he likes. He stays 1d6 weeks.
  • Fire, minor: a large fire sweeps a city, town or village, destroying 10%-40% of a city's buildings, 50%-70% of a town's, or 80%-100% of a village's. Building materials cost double. Fortunately, little life is lost. Minor fires are a handy way for the DM to change the buildings or daily life of a familiar place.
  • Flooding: sudden and less severe than a flood (the yearly event; the book prints "Table 70: Yearly Events"). A levee, dam or dike collapses, or a cloudburst strikes upstream. The water rushes down the river bed in a wave 5d4 feet high and 101-200 feet wide, for 1d6 miles before losing force. It snaps trees, tears down buildings and sweeps men away: anyone in its path is swept to his death unless he has a raft or something else that floats. Afterward the water quickly falls to 3d12 inches, and stays there until the broken works are rebuilt or it evaporates.
  • Haunting: rumor says some site has lately seen strange supernatural events, often a battlefield, murder or accident. The DM decides whether it is real; many creatures in this book suit a haunted site. A ready-made adventure: simple or elaborate, perhaps with a spirit returning to finish some hard task or to right a wrong (done, perhaps, by the provincial magistrate).
  • Horrendous monster: a powerful, evil creature moves in and terrorizes the villages. The DM picks it, from this book or others. Its lair is somewhere secluded, hidden from hunters, but the peasants know roughly where, and don't attack it for fear. If it isn't beaten or driven off soon, the villagers make offerings to it as an evil god, and more of its kind (or its young) appear, making things worse.
  • Incursion, major: a strong force moves in to make a permanent home. It may or may not be friendly. Its size suits the territory, as with the yearly event, but this is a sudden arrival, not a slow migration: invading or retreating soldiers, refugees from disaster or war, bandits or monsters driven from another province, nomads following game, even prospectors chasing a new strike.
  • Incursion, minor: the same as a major incursion with a much smaller force: a band of ninja spying on the province, reinforcements for a bandit gang, a punitive expedition from a neighboring warlord, a raiding party of monsters.
  • Injustice: wickedness takes over the local government and courts: corrupt, greedy magistrates and officials jail and punish innocents, because the magistrate was bribed, wants the accused's property, was tricked, is cruel, or is taking official revenge on rebels or traitors. It can be stopped if evidence reaches higher officials (if they aren't corrupt too), or if the characters protect the innocent. 5% chance a character is wrongly accused of a crime (20% if he has a powerful enemy).
  • Landslide: only in hills or mountains. A landslide or avalanche blocks a main road of the province until cleared. Peasants are called out to clear it, which takes 1-2 weeks unless spells speed the work.
  • Maiden of virtue: a young woman of exceptional grace, wit and beauty appears in the region: a powerful noble's daughter (50%), a maiden of mysterious and magical origin (30%), an exiled princess (10%), or simply a commoner (10%). She charms and impresses everyone. Her fine handwriting shows her pure nature; she plays musical instruments and has other artistic gifts; she respects her parents (if she has any). Unless she is a powerful noble's daughter, she can be courted (and perhaps married) without full formalities. Aware but not vain of her qualities, she won't accept just anyone: her suitor must himself be a model of virtue, skilled in the arts, and heroic. Even to catch her notice he must make an artistic item of quality (a poem, painting, exceptional handwriting), and he needs comeliness and charisma of at least 13 each. A mysterious maiden or a princess may set impossible tasks for a suitor. Social rank matters less than these qualities. The DM handles the courtship, the attraction between them and the outcome.
  • Major battle: a large, important battle is fought in the region. The DM decides the forces and site; the book strongly recommends mass-combat rules, perhaps giving the characters command of units. Otherwise the DM decides the outcome. Before it, many troops move through the area (perhaps many interesting encounters). After it, the losers retreat, perhaps flee; many peasants take up arms to protect their villages and hunt down the losers, and the winners' patrols sweep the countryside for stragglers, deserters and small enemy bands.
  • Maneater: a leopard, tiger, wolf or similar beast has acquired a taste for human flesh and raids the villages, carrying off women, children and farmers from their fields once or twice a week and dragging them into the woods. The villagers are frozen with fear, won't go out alone or after dark, and beg the government, a powerful non-player character or the characters for help. It keeps hunting until caught or killed.
  • Marriage: a character courting someone has his or her proposal accepted (unless the DM rules otherwise). If not, an important person in the region marries or arranges a child's marriage; characters known to him are invited. Either way there is feasting and celebration.
  • Notorious criminal: a wanted villain is rumored to be in the area: a banished lord secretly returned, a traitor fleeing the emperor's wrath, an escaped convict, a famous bandit. There may be a reward for his capture or death. Or it may be only rumor and a wild goose chase.
  • Plague: see Plague under yearly events.
  • Recruiting: soldiers are needed, and special measures are taken: forced levies of peasants, bounties for capable officers, and recruiting gangs. 20% chance the characters are swept up by a gang; if they don't want to be hustled off to the front, they will need some fast talking (or something).
  • Troop movements: organized soldiers, friendly or enemy (or both at different times), sweep through the province, looting and collecting rice, grain and horses with no repayment, though notes may be issued. 10% chance any character is arrested as a spy. Ninja characters are ordered to spy on the enemy 40% of the time. Friendly troops don't pillage wholesale, nor (usually) do enemy troops; barbarians and raiding enemies burn buildings and do as much damage as they can, besides carrying off anything valuable.
  • Uprising: the peasants rise against their lot, protesting injustice, taxes or general misfortune. It starts in a village or two and spreads quickly through the countryside.
    • They arm themselves with farm tools and weapons taken from samurai they have hunted down; only 10% have proper armor. 60% chance any monastery in the area supports them with troops, shelter and aid.
    • They have no plan, simply attacking and ambushing government troops and officials. A strong leader could train them into an effective force in 2-4 months.
    • The government sends reinforcements and shows no mercy, so the peasants fight to the death. Characters may lead the rising or command government troops. Unless the characters tip the balance, it fails, and everyone who took part (and their families) is executed if caught.
    • It may not be in vain: 70% chance the government listens and responds, perhaps lowering taxes or replacing officials. And 70% chance of more bandit activity for 1-3 months as survivors flee to the hills.
    • As with war and rebellion, the DM decides the size and kind of forces; the book recommends mass-combat rules.
  • Vengeful stranger: a mysterious non-player character arrives, making quiet inquiries in the villages and towns for someone he means to take revenge on for some old wrong (perhaps a murder or insult). If the characters have offended or wronged a family or person in the past, he is looking for them, and finds out where they are 70% of the time. If not, he may ask their help in his search (or his quarry may). Local officials usually stay out of it, but the DM may have them step in to end the feud. If he is hunting the characters and they beat him, it starts a feud between the two families for generations.
  • VIP visit: an important official makes a formal visit to the province, for a reason the DM decides. If he has come to investigate the local officials' misdeeds, he travels in disguise, and they will certainly try to get rid of him; characters may be hired to protect him or to kill him. Otherwise there are official banquets and feasts (the characters may be invited).

Roll the maximum number of times on the column for where the characters are that day: three rolls in the wilderness, for instance. Many rolls will give no event (01-50 is always no event). A lonely mountain pass uses the wilderness column; once they come down into farms and villages, the rural column. When a result is Monster, roll on the encounter table for the terrain: the "OA Encounters" roll tables in the OA Tables compendium, by terrain and climate.

The daily events

  • Bandits: by accident or design, the characters find a camp or outpost of a bandit band. If bandits are active in the area, they reach the edge of the camp: 2d10 bandits try to delay or waylay them while two run to the main camp for help or to raise the alarm. If not, they meet an advance party of 3d10 mounted bandit scouts, who avoid a fight if they can and may pose as travelers; if the bandits are clever and the players aren't, the ruse works and nothing more happens.
  • Bandit camp: the characters stumble on a bandit camp in the wilderness. The DM builds it from the information in the MM.
  • Becalmed: the wind dies and the sea goes perfectly still. Ships can't sail today and must be rowed.
  • Contest: characters of noble rank are invited by a powerful lord to a contest in an art (poetry, painting, calligraphy and so on) that at least one of them is proficient in, at a set time and place. It takes the form of a formal party: each guest composes a work on the spot, judged on its quality, how well it suits the occasion, its imagery and its sheer beauty. The winner gets a minor gift and gains honor. Characters can miss it for good reason (leaving town on their lord's orders and so on); without one, they lose 2 honor, as people assume they are ashamed of their skill. (See Contests on the Peaceful Proficiencies page.)
  • Crime: a crime, petty or notorious, touches the characters: they may be friends of the victim or the accused (or the victims), witnesses, or asked or ordered to help catch the criminal. A good start for an adventure.
  • Duel: a character is challenged to a duel, perhaps for an accidental insult or public embarrassment, by someone who has heard of his fame, through mistaken identity, or over an old score with him or his family. Shukenja are never normally challenged.
  • Entreaty: a lower-ranking noble or a group of commoners asks the characters a special favor. A noble may want them to recommend him to a non-player character they know, or do something beyond his rank or power, and will pay or even bribe them. Peasants may want warriors to protect their village from bandits, drive off an evil spirit, or avenge a wrong. A good start for an adventure.
  • Fire, small: a fire breaks out in a building near the characters, and they are expected to help fight it, by organizing or joining the bucket line. If they are at home, one of their own buildings is burning. 70% of the time it was set on purpose: by an enemy, by ninja creating a distraction to slip past them, or by a malicious spirit. If not fought quickly and well, it burns out of control, and an out-of-control fire has a 70% chance of spreading to nearby buildings.
  • Haunting: see Haunting under monthly events.
  • Illness: a dangerous disease strikes a character (20%) or a non-player character they know (80%). Signs start today. Roll 2d6 for the days it runs. Each untreated day the patient gets worse: high fever, sweating, dizziness, weakness. If it isn't cured by the end, he saves versus death: on a failure he dies; on a success he begins to recover. A sick character must rest one day for each day he was ill.
  • Insult: a character insults a non-player character, on purpose or by accident. If the other is of equal or higher rank, he demands satisfaction. At court, the offended party complains to the ruling lord, who acts on it. If that punishment isn't enough, or the offended party is of lower rank, the character has made a lasting enemy who will try to harm him later.
  • Invitation: the characters get an order, politely worded as an invitation, to call on a powerful lord. The DM decides why: to celebrate a birth, christening, marriage or new office; an outing to view the moon, admire cherry blossoms or hunt; political maneuvers (special instructions, embarrassing a third party, compromising the characters); or, rarely, a purely social call. These are never casual: proper manners and respect are required throughout, and refusing without good reason is an insult.
  • Kidnapping: someone tries to kidnap a character or a non-player character they know: ninja sent by a powerful lord to get someone out of the way or force cooperation, bandits or yakuza after ransom, a jealous lover removing a rival, or even two lovers secretly running off under cover of a kidnapping. It can lead to further adventures.
  • Land: land is sighted: depending on where the ship is, the coast of their destination, an island on their course, or a small uncharted island, which is sure to be full of strange and dangerous creatures (perhaps even dinosaurs and gargantua).
  • Monster: roll on the encounter table for the terrain.
  • Mystery: something strange or supernatural happens nearby; the characters see it or hear of it. The DM describes it; it may be the work of spirits, a powerful spellcaster, a cunning creature or even a deity. 60% chance the characters are asked to investigate.
  • Nobles: a noble party of 2d10 bushi, 1d6 samurai and 1-3 persons of rank. 80% of the time they travel openly, on foot with the nobles in palanquins, and expect every respect due their rank. 20% of the time they travel in disguise, perhaps on a secret mission or fleeing a powerful enemy: on foot dressed as peasants (and forced to swallow their pride and act humbly), or mounted and dressed as wandering samurai and bushi.
  • Pirates: 1-3 wako ships are sighted. See Wako in the OA Monsters compendium.
  • Plot: the characters learn of a plot against their lord or a powerful non-player character they know. What they do with it is up to them; a good basis for an adventure.
  • Ruins: the characters find ruins. The DM picks the kind or rolls on "OA Ruins" in the OA Tables compendium: 01-10 temple compound (70%), 11-60 farmhouse (20%), 61-90 shrine (50%), 91-100 military stockade (30%). The percentage is the chance the ruin is haunted by a spirit or home to a monster; if so, the DM decides what is there.
  • Ship: a sail on the horizon. 30% chance it is a ghost ship, carrying the dead to their new land. Otherwise it is a merchant ship (50%) or a warship (20%), and either has a 10% chance of a gajin crew on the long, dangerous voyage (or blown hopelessly off course).
  • Shrine: a small shrine to a local deity. Characters who stop and make proper offerings have a 10% chance of the benefits of a bless spell for 24 hours. Characters who damage it or are disrespectful, on purpose or not, have an 80% chance of being struck by a curse of the DM's devising.
  • Special: one or more characters get a special mission from their lord, mentor or family head: a ninja's mission, information a yakuza must get, a quest for a shukenja, an important message for a samurai to deliver. A good start for an adventure.
  • Storm: a fierce storm. At sea: gale winds, driving rain and huge waves for 5d6 hours. On land: a storm to suit the season, with driving rain, lightning and fierce wind, or whipping snow, bitter cold and wind; in deserts, a sandstorm. Either way the characters can't travel today because of drifts, flooding, dunes and so on. Being out in it is exhausting: exposed characters take 1-2 points of damage an hour.
  • Stranger: an unknown non-player character takes an unusual interest in the party: an ordinary traveler (30%), a member of a secret society (10%), an official of the secret police (10%), a ninja on a mission (10%), a noble in disguise (10%), a bandit wanting the characters as cover (10%), a hengeyokai or spirit in human form (10%), or a yakuza quietly gathering information (10%). He is heading their way and usually wants to travel with them for company and safety. Whether he is a threat is up to the DM.
  • Traveler: someone going the same way, with no special interest in the characters, who travels with them a little way if allowed: a peasant going to the next village, a runner for a secret society, a samurai carrying a message, a bushi looking for work. The DM decides.
  • VIP: a noble or important official passes through on a state visit, openly, with 20d6 bushi, 10d4 samurai and servants. They go ahead through the streets announcing his title and forcing commoners aside with blows and drawn weapons; anyone bold enough to challenge them is cut down on the spot. Everyone is expected to get out of sight or bow as he passes.
