The Celestial Emperor and his bureaucracy

Elsewhere people tend to see nonhuman creatures as a loose crowd of beings with no order. In the Eastern Lands the world is seen as one ordered whole. One strong belief is in the Celestial Emperor, a mighty being who heads the Celestial Bureaucracy, a government of the spirits. Many spirit creatures in the OA Monsters compendium serve him, and many hold offices in his bureaucracy, where they take and carry out orders, punish the wicked and file reports. The chiang lung (river dragons), for instance, are charged with making rain and report to the Ministry of Thunder, which reports to the Celestial Emperor. Like officials anywhere, these spirits can be corrupt, disobedient, just or incompetent, and they can be replaced, since their superiors review their work and conduct every year.

Source: OA p.136-137 (An Overview of The Eastern Lands; Geography; Population; Shou Lung; T'u Lung; Wa; Kozakura). Rewritten in plain words; names checked against the page image.

The Eastern Lands are a vast continent with a huge range of climates, lands, governments, societies, cultures and beliefs; describing it fully would take another book this size. This is a broad overview of the main lands, as a starting point for a campaign.

There are four main empires: Shou Lung, T'u Lung, Kozakura and Wa. Around them are many lesser powers: uncivilized tribes, tribal confederations, warlords' domains, petty kingdoms and trading posts. Many ally with powerful neighbors when it suits them; others, feisty and rebellious, keep their independence as best they can. Between the settled lands lie stretches of harsh, empty wilderness, home only to a few hardy settlers, bandits, dangerous head-hunters, nonhuman peoples and monsters.

Geography, north to south

  • The Land of Snow Demons: in the far north, endless permafrost tundra broken only by a few stunted trees and heaved-up rock. Winters are long and very harsh, summers short and cool.
  • The Ama Basin: south of the permafrost, thick swampy woods, mostly pine with thorny berries, moss and ferns, rich in game (deer, moose, elk, bear, fox, rabbit). The land rises southward to the Koryaz Mountains, a series of low ranges. Waters flow in from north and south, forming streams, lakes and swamps that feed the Ama River, which drains into the north end of the Celestial Sea. In spring, swollen with melting snow, the Ama becomes a raging torrent.
  • The Desert of Horses (the Beastlands): beyond rugged foothills at the basin's southwest end lie dry steppes, thousands of square miles of flat, featureless land broken now and then by rocky outcrops.
  • Wa and Kozakura: northeast of the Ama Basin, the continent curves around the north end of the Celestial Sea and sends a mountainous peninsula south. Off its tip lie rugged islands, including Wa and Kozakura, given a mild temperate climate by warm southern currents.
  • The Chukei Plateau: south of the Koryaz Mountains, a high plain forms Shou Lung's northern provinces of Chukei and Pyint'sien. Once fertile meadow, changing weather and poor land management have left it a dusty, cold, windswept plateau. To the west the Koryaz Mountains curve south and fall away into foothills, a barrier between the plateau and the Desert of Horses; to the east the plateau drops in steep escarpments to the Celestial Sea.
  • The Three-River Basin: further south, the plateau slopes into rolling hills and down to the main river basin of the Eastern Lands. To the east are fertile, well-watered floodplains. Three great rivers, the Ch'ing Tung, the Hungsete and the Fenghsintzu, tumble from the western mountains through the hills to the Celestial Sea. The weather is warm and temperate, sub-tropical along the south side.
  • The Peerless Mountains (Wu Pi Te Shan Mo): to the west and southwest, rising to towering heights, with warm, humid, lush lower slopes and jagged, frozen peaks.
  • The south: beyond the Three-River Basin the land rises again into rugged rolling country, lush and green under the yearly monsoons. The coast swings southeast, marking the lower end of the Celestial Sea. The hills run south and southeast, rising into a chain of volcanoes. The climate turns fully tropical, with thick jungles full of strange and fanciful creatures, feathery peninsulas reaching into the Eastern Ocean, and chains of islands.

Peoples

  • Most people live in the Three-River Basin and its foothills, and on Wa and Kozakura.
  • Shou Lung centers on the Three-River Basin and stretches west and north. Feeding its huge population takes nearly all the basin's farmland; herding and a little farming go on on the Chukei Plateau, and the Peerless and Koryaz mountains are mined for ores sent downriver or overland.
  • T'u Lung lies along the south and southwest of the basin, farming mainly along the Fenghsintzu, with farming and lumbering in the southern hills.
  • The Ama Basin is home to nomadic hunting tribes who farm little but herd elk and reindeer. The few human tribes of the Land of Snow Demons live by hunting seal, bear and reindeer.
  • The Desert of Horses holds several tribes of nomadic horsemen in a loose confederation. A strong leader has lately arisen among them and is slowly forging them into a fierce warrior nation.
  • The northeast peninsula has several petty kingdoms that pay tribute to Shou Lung. The islands between it and Wa and Kozakura hold tribes of primitive fishers and hunters.
  • Wa and Kozakura are home to a people different from the mainlanders, most likely an offshoot that settled the islands in ancient times.
  • The southern jungles: south of the basin the people thin out to isolated jungle tribes. Those on the coast trade widely with the civilized north and have formed small states that pay tribute to T'u Lung or Shou Lung. Deep in the jungle lie the remains of an ancient empire that once ruled all the south, under evil snake creatures (possibly yuan-ti), which corrupted and changed several of the human peoples it touched.

Shou Lung

Shou Lung ("Receiver of the Dragon") is the largest and most powerful empire, and the oldest state, in existence in one form or another for over 1,200 years. Apart from a few times of turmoil, an emperor has always ruled it; the present one is Emperor Chin of the Kuo Dynasty, the eighth to rule. Thousands of officials, major and minor, run its bureaucracy, chosen by examinations held throughout the land, so even the poorest commoner can rise to influence if he is talented and studies hard.

  • It has 14 provinces, each under a governor, divided into districts, each with its own official. At every level, officials oversee those below them, hear court cases, keep the peace, collect taxes and build public works.
  • Well-kept roads and bridges link the provinces and carry steady trade. Imperial Messengers, posted at stations throughout the land, carry news to and from the capital, T'ien Shih.
  • Dikes and dams along the great rivers reduce the risk of floods.
  • Regular coins and paper money are minted and honored everywhere.

T'u Lung

T'u Lung ("Earth Dragon") was part of Shou Lung until a quarrel over the imperial succession 300 years ago, when it set up its own emperor and court. After many wars things have settled, but there is no love lost between the two empires.

  • In the succession wars, T'u Lung's emperor was backed by powerful officials and nobles of the rebel provinces, who gained great power. The government copies Shou Lung's, but the emperor (of the Lui Dynasty) has never broken his nobles' power.
  • The nobles control the examinations and have made many offices hereditary, and have exempted their estates from most imperial edicts, taxes included. The emperor can enforce an edict only with the consent of most of the nobles.
  • Commoners have little chance to rise, and corruption in office is common. The people are easily oppressed and have no recourse to the law.
  • There are six provinces, each under a hereditary governor, divided into districts whose posts go by family and bribery. The public works inherited from Shou Lung are poorly kept and new ones seldom built.
  • Political plotting is the main business of the capital, Chia Wan Ch'uan, and many nobles lead secret societies sworn to overthrow the emperor.

Wa

The island of Wa is a unified military state. It has an emperor, but the title is honorary; real power lies with the shogun ("barbarian-suppressing general"), always of the Hidetomi family.

  • The shogun grants the island's fiefs to daimyos, each with total control of his land as long as he obeys and carries out the shogun's orders. The shogun's court deals only with threats to its power and disputes between fiefs, but the shogun can confiscate land or move a daimyo to another fief, which helps his family keep control. In return for his fief, a daimyo owes military service and governs his land.
  • Warriors, above all samurai, rank above everyone. Each daimyo keeps a household of samurai paid in rice, who owe him absolute, loyal service. Below the warriors come peasants, then craftsmen, then merchants, and strict laws keep the classes apart.
  • Cities are divided into walled wards; residents pass through armed gates to visit other parts of the city and must be back in their own ward by night.
  • Samurai have special privileges suited to their military upbringing, above all the vendetta and the right to avenge insults.
  • Travel is strictly controlled, and it is hard to leave or enter the island. All these laws exist to stop any rebellion or civil war against the shogun.

Kozakura

Kozakura ("Little Cherry Blossom") is home to the same people as Wa, with almost the same customs and traditions, but it is far from unified. For centuries powerful daimyos have fought without end for the title of shogun over its fiefs and estates. It is turbulent, a place where even someone of the humblest birth can win fortune and power: perfect for an adventurer seeking fame and fortune.

  • Right now several powerful daimyos back the emperor's bid to regain his long-lost political power, against what is left of the bakufu (the shogun's government). Each side is trying to win over the other families, some out of loyalty, some to gain power for themselves, and some are arranging alliances with both sides so they can't lose.
  • Warriors are the most respected and powerful class, but Kozakura lacks Wa's rigid laws, and more than once a humble peasant has risen to be a mighty lord through skill at arms.

Source: OA p.137 (Gajin). Rewritten in plain words.

Players with other 1eFRPG books may want to bring characters of the standard classes (fighter, magic-user, cleric, thief and so on) into the Eastern Lands. These lands are very different from theirs. They are inward-looking and closed, avoiding the outside world when they can. Trade with outsiders exists but is infrequent and carefully controlled, and many who travel the sea lanes and caravan routes with gold and treasure vanish at the hands of bandits or crueler dangers.

This isolation has left the people with two traits. They have little curiosity about the rest of the world, which most of them think is full of rude, hostile barbarians (gajin) with nothing worth dealing for. And they believe they are superior: that all gajin fall below their own culture and refinement. So a character of another class who arrives here, by a long sea voyage or a hard overland trip, finds his level and class mean little to the people. He is gajin, an uncivilized outsider.

Disadvantages

  • No place in society: people don't know where gajin fit in the caste system. A gajin who can show a rank equal to one of the local classes is treated as a member of that class, though always with a hint of contempt: a fighter who can show he serves a great lord at home is treated like a samurai, but never gets a samurai's full recognition.
  • No family: gajin have no family or clan and can never gain the benefits of one, as OA characters do.
  • Much to relearn: his own common tongue isn't the trade language here, so he must learn it to talk with anyone. Clothes are different, and he must learn proper styles and patterns of dress. Armor is different, and he needs instruction before using it. The whole fabric of society is different, and on his own he must watch constantly to avoid countless social blunders and outrages.

Advantages

  • His abilities are unchanged: moving to a new land doesn't change what he can do; his powers still work here.
  • No honor: as an outsider, the OA code of honor has no bearing on him. That doesn't mean he has no honor, but gajin characters don't use the OA honor rules.
  • A novelty: a gajin who behaves in a civilized, proper way may find himself the honored guest of one or more lords, who gain great honor by sponsoring him, and be closer to those in power than his place in society would otherwise allow.

Nonhumans

The nonhumans of other 1eFRPG books are even stranger to the people here. Other gajin are at least human; these are wholly unknown. They are often mistaken for hairy men, spirit folk or wandering spirits, and now and then attacked by people who take them for dangerous, evil creatures. Either way, they are a novelty.

Source: OA p.138-140 (Daily Life in The Eastern Lands; Dress; Food; Buildings). Rewritten in plain words.

Life in the Eastern Lands, and in the real lands that inspired them, differs from what most players know in dress, food, customs and behavior. Each difference is small, but together they make a way of life foreign to most players. These pages describe some of them to help the DM and players catch the feel and color of the world. They can't cover everything; the DM is strongly encouraged to read more about the real cultures behind the setting.

Nothing here is absolute. The real lands behind the setting hold many cultures, more still across different periods, and what is true in one place may be quite different in another. This is a fantasy world, and the DM should change it as he likes.

Dress

Clothes keep people warm and dry, and almost as importantly they show rank and status. Nearly all clothing is decorated with dyed patterns or embroidery, but the kind of garment, the quality of the decoration and the material all mark the wearer's standing.

  • Materials: mostly cotton and silk. Other materials, usually local and for the lower classes, include pounded bark, flax, wool, woven horsehair, furs, paper and hemp. Heavy leather is used for durability, soft leather like deerskin for flexibility or rich decoration. Primitive tribesmen and poor commoners use whatever is cheapest and most at hand.
  • Colors: white is usually the color of mourning, so nearly all cloth is dyed. Browns, ochres, yellows, grays and blues are common; brighter greens, pinks and reds are rarer and worn by people of higher rank. Dyes come from flowers, nuts, bark, woods and certain minerals.
  • Trousers and robes: the most common garment is a pair of short, loose cotton trousers that wrap the waist and tie with strings, loose or tied snug at the leg, so they can be pulled up for wading paddies and streams. Often striped or patterned, they are worn by peasants of both sexes. Commoners wear a short robe over them, belted. Wealthier, more important people often skip the trousers and wear one or more long robes.
  • Layers: nobles wear layered robes, each a different color showing at the sleeve ends and collar; arranging the colors and order is an art for many court ladies. Robes have wide, open sleeves, for beauty and use: in cold weather they serve as muffs (gloves aren't usually worn), and they hold a handkerchief or a string of cash. Robes are often richly dyed, brocaded and embroidered, and can be valuable. In cold seasons people add more and heavier layers, with a quilted cotton coat against the wind, and take layers off as the day warms. In rain, peasants wear a simple straw raincape (mino).
  • Footwear: the simplest and most common is a woven straw sandal, cheap, durable and easy to make. In Kozakura, sandals of straw or wooden blocks are worn by all. In Shou Lung and T'u Lung, refined people wear soft leather or cloth slippers and soldiers short soft leather boots, while commoners wear sandals, since they can't afford to ruin good shoes in muddy fields. In the cold north, the usual shoe is a leather boot wrapped in fur leggings against snow and ice.
  • Hats clearly show status, and nearly everyone has one. Peasants' hats are practical: round, broad-brimmed straw or bamboo that keeps off the sun and doubles as a basket. Wandering shukenja and monks may wear hats like these, or basket-like hats that cover the whole head. Nobles' hats are often small, their style showing the wearer's position. In some places gentlemen wear huge brimmed horsehair hats. A scarf or cloth keeps off the rain.
  • Beauty: men, especially of rank, pride themselves on grace and beauty: a pale complexion is best, some even pluck their eyebrows, and perfumes are common (people of worth are often skilled at blending them). Most men fall short, weathered by life. Women blacken their teeth (a pearly white smile is an unfortunate flaw), pluck their eyebrows and repaint them as a fine thin line, and powder their faces as pale as possible.
  • Hair shows age and status. Men of rank draw their hair back into a topknot held with carved pins or a cord, a privilege generally kept for nobles, warriors and the ruling class. In some places, especially Kozakura, cutting off a man's topknot is a punishment for minor offenses, a sign he has shamed himself before his lord. Small children are often shaved bald but for one lock (on the crown for boys, over the ear for girls), then grow a full head of hair. Young warriors tie theirs in a topknot, and at his coming of age a samurai youth shaves the top of his forehead to show he is a man. Peasant men wear their hair loose or in a long queue. Women grow theirs long and flowing, perhaps gathered into elaborate headdresses; its length and richness measure her beauty and station. In mourning or grief, or on becoming a nun, a woman cuts her hair short. Men entering the priesthood shave their heads.

Food

  • Rice is the one constant throughout the civilized lands, served in some form with almost every meal. In Shou Lung and T'u Lung people greet each other not with "Hello" but "Have you eaten rice today?" Rice is boiled as a main dish, cooked into gruel, mixed (leftover) with meat and vegetables, vinegared, shaped and served cold, pounded into rice cakes, ground into flour for buns and noodles, and fermented into sake, a strong drink. It is the stuff of life, as wheat is elsewhere.
  • Poor man's grains and beans: where rice is scarce or too costly for the everyday table, people eat yellow millet, sorghum or barley, pounded into cakes or cooked into thick gruel. Beans of many kinds (soy, red, black, brown) are eaten with or instead of rice, stewed or mashed into paste that may be fermented, flavored, dried or sweetened and used as a dip, a bun filling, candy or sauce. Soybeans give tofu (bean "milk" curdled and pressed into soft cakes, then stewed, dried, deep-fried and so on) and soy sauce, a thin salty sauce made by mashing, fermenting, soaking and rinsing, used to flavor almost anything.
  • Vegetables come next, grown in family plots and stewed, fried, pickled or steamed, almost never raw except as garnish. There are also many fruits, nuts, grasses and flowers: bamboo shoots, water chestnut roots, melons, giant radishes, many mushrooms, bean sprouts, pumpkins, squash, chestnuts, potatoes, cucumbers, turnips, cabbage, onions, leeks, peaches, pears, persimmons, sweet potatoes, carrots, walnuts, almonds, lychees, lotus root, plums, cherries, bananas, peanuts and many more. Unusual dishes include pickled greens or radishes (often with chilies), pickled plums (almost anything is pickled), dried flower buds, dried chestnuts and pastes.
  • Seafood: people near the sea, rivers or lakes eat hundreds of kinds of fish, common to exotic. Delicacies include pufferfish (deadly poisonous if wrongly prepared), sea cucumber, jellyfish, octopus, eels, shrimp and fish maw. Kelp is dried for soups and flavoring. Nearly everything from the sea is used.
  • Meat: fish is the main meat, then chicken and pork, cooked many ways, and game when available. Beef is seldom eaten, as cattle are rare and specially regarded. Barbarians eat mutton and horsemeat, especially at feasts.
  • Drink: tea is the most common drink, in many varieties, usually plain; nomads mix it with milk and sugar and even serve it as soup. Rice wines (sake and the like) are served warm in small cups, and beer with meals. Steppe peoples drink fermented mare's milk, which they call a refreshing tonic, mixed with mare's blood on special occasions, especially for warriors before or after battle. Steppe warriors use a great deal of milk; elsewhere it is rare.
  • A day's meals in town: in the morning, steamed buns, dumplings, rice or rice gruel and several pickles; at midday the biggest meal, with rice, vegetables, perhaps fish or chicken, more pickles and tea; late in the day, tea with rice candies or sweet buns; in the evening, a light meal of rice and a few simple delicacies.
  • On the road: before breaking camp, rice gruel, plain rice, millet or barley; at midday, if there is time, rice cake, cold rice, or a packet of rice, fish, nuts and dried seaweed or pickles tied in banana leaves, with fruit if any; in the evening, more rice with dried fish and fresh or dried vegetables, or fresh game if the day's hunting went well.

Buildings

There are three main kinds of building: commoners' homes, the palaces of the rich and powerful, and temples, plus military buildings. (The book includes several floorplans; they aren't reproduced here.)

  • Wooden peasant house: at its simplest, one large room with an earth floor and open rafters, under a thick, steep thatched roof that sheds snow and rain, with broad eaves for shade and shelter. Windows have wooden lattices, removable shutters, bamboo shades or oiled paper. A small veranda, as wide as the eaves and often covered with straw mats, runs around the outside. Inside, an earthen hearth (usually a stone-lined pit) dominates, with a hook above for cooking pots, especially rice; smoke leaves by a hole in the roof. There is no other heating, so family life centers on the hearth, especially in winter.
  • Larger houses add raised wooden platforms beside the earth-floored hearth area for sleeping and other activities, separated by removable paper screens or fixed wooden walls, with storage built into the walls and under the platforms. An attic, reached by a broad-stepped ladder, may store goods and house the younger family members.
  • Roofs: thatch needs constant care; wealthier homes use glazed tile, costlier but durable, and now a sign of status. Roof ridges and eave edges are often decorated with wooden forms and carvings.
  • In cities and large towns houses are packed tightly along narrow, winding streets. Thatch is hard to come by, so most roofs are tile, and thatch marks a truly poor man. Most shops are in the family home: by day, big front shutters fold down into a table for goods. Behind a row of houses there may be a shared courtyard and well. Larger, richer homes are set back behind walled gardens or built around a central courtyard. Houses are seldom more than one story.
  • Outbuildings: workshops, stables and granaries are usually built like the house, except granaries, which are almost always plaster and stone because of fire: a house can be rebuilt, but the wealth in a burned granary's rice can never be replaced.
  • Fire: buildings of wood, thatch and paper burn easily, and fire is greatly feared, especially in cities, where wind carries sparks from building to building and fires sweep whole districts. Every ward has organized fire-fighting teams, usually under a noble, but their methods are primitive: bucket lines, and pulling down nearby buildings to stop the spread.
  • Clay brick house: used where good timber is scarce, usually two stories, often around a central courtyard or with a walled garden. Cooking is done in a kitchen built around a clay or brick stove. With no other heating, charcoal braziers warm rooms in cold weather. Roofs are often flat (used as decks) or gently sloped and tiled. Nearly every room has windows with wooden lattices or heavy removable shutters. Red-painted ornaments (red is lucky) are common. Being mostly plaster, clay and stone, these houses resist fire far better.
  • Nobles' and rich men's houses are like peasants' but larger and grander, with many rooms (to show wealth and status, and to house the lord's retainers, servants and wives) and extensive landscaped gardens, often with a man-made pond or stream. They have solid wooden floors and rooms divided by movable screens, and are always walled, for privacy and for protection in wars and revolts.
  • Temples are grand: usually a group of buildings in one walled compound, mostly of wood, though splendid towers (pagodas) are often stone. The temple stands on a raised foundation with stone terraces and a broad veranda under wide tiled eaves. Inside, a great hall is dominated by an imposing statue or artifacts of the deity, with smaller rooms for the priests. The grounds are landscaped with flowering and ornamental trees.
  • Castles differ in style from gajin castles but are alike in many ways. A castle sits on the most commanding or strategic ground. At its center is a main building many stories tall, like a gajin keep and likewise the last line of defense, on a foundation of heavy stone blocks higher than a man, reached by ramps and stairs. Around it are lesser towers and walls with few gates opening onto narrow winding passages, pierced with loopholes for shooting at attackers. Around all that are ditches or moats, more walls and more towers. Besieging a castle is a formidable task.

Source: OA p.140-141 (Religion; Law and Justice). Rewritten in plain words.

Religion

The ordinary person doesn't attend a temple regularly, and the idea of a "church" set apart from all others is strange to him. That doesn't mean he isn't pious and respectful, or that temples and monasteries are disorganized; the attitude to religion is simply very different.

  • There are several religions, each with its own beliefs and practices: The Way, The Path of Enlightenment, The Eight Million Gods, ancestor worship, the cult of the state and more. Each teaches enlightenment, perfection and salvation in its own way, and each believes it is right.
  • Few common people follow only one. Taking no chances, not wanting to offend any deity, they make offerings, hear sermons, keep holy days and pray at temples of many religions, and no one thinks this odd or wrong.
  • Compared with gajin faiths, the religions are extremely tolerant of one another. Several are practiced in the same area, temples often side by side. A sect may adopt practices or forms from another, explained anew by its own beliefs; minor gods may be taken in as forms of a deity it already worships.
  • Priests are faithful to their own religion and practice no other. They would like the peasants to follow only their teaching, and work at it, but know common folk follow many beliefs at once.
  • Religions are often split into sects that share goals and beliefs but disagree on the best way to pursue them: one chants a phrase over and over, another insists on a different phrase, a third gives up chanting for breathing and physical exercises. Each thinks its way is right, and fierce rivalries often lead to feuds and violent clashes. Sects of the same religion are often more hostile to each other than to entirely different religions.

Law and justice

Most of the Eastern Lands are civilized and orderly, and much effort goes into keeping order and harmony, with regular laws, courts and punishments. Exact laws and punishments differ from country to country, but the workings of justice are much the same everywhere.

  • The court: there is generally one in every province and major city, headed by a magistrate with broad powers. He may be a scholar who passed the examinations, a noble appointed by the emperor, the province's daimyo, a learned sage or the village headman. His officers are the bailiff and the constables, who may hire outcasts as helpers, and he may have one or more secretaries.
  • Before trial: the bailiff and constables gather the evidence; physical evidence is held at the court until the trial. Witnesses and anyone involved can be arrested and held, or ordered to appear. There is no protection from arrest except the possible displeasure of the magistrate or higher authorities, which can make arresting important or powerful people very hard. Once everything is gathered, trial follows quickly.
  • The trial: accuser and accused each state their case. There are no lawyers; the magistrate asks all the questions. A reluctant party can be beaten or tortured on his order to help his memory, and the same awaits anyone out of order. Witnesses are questioned likewise, and force can be used to get their testimony. The bailiff keeps order, produces witnesses and gives the beatings.
  • Magic in court: in a murder case, a spellcaster may be called to speak with the dead victim, and that testimony is accepted as fact. Spells may also test the truth of testimony. After hearing everything, the magistrate decides, helped by his secretaries, who cite the laws and earlier cases.
  • Rank: people of higher rank, having greater responsibilities, often get special treatment. Acts that are crimes for commoners often aren't for the warrior class: in lands like Kozakura, a samurai may cut down a commoner he finds insulting or truculent without being charged with murder, and with proper approval may pursue a vendetta for a slain relative. But they are punished more harshly for things less criminal in commoners: gambling and drunkenness are far worse crimes for a samurai, because he has broken a trust.
  • Punishments are fixed by law, but the magistrate can interpret it and make a punishment lighter or harsher. For commoners: execution, branding, loss of the hands, fines, prison, banishment, slavery, wearing a heavy yoke, and public proclamation of the crime. For the upper classes: house arrest, banishment, loss of position and honorable death. For especially vile crimes such as treason, a samurai may be humiliated by public execution.
  • Civil cases: the magistrate hears civil and criminal cases alike, but since the courts treat even the innocent harshly, most people try to settle civil disputes without them, through a mediator (a priest or village headman) who sets the terms; both sides must agree. If that fails, the case may go to court.
  • Collective responsibility: to discourage crime and treachery, many governments hold a criminal's whole family, village or group responsible for his acts. A banished samurai's whole family may be banished with him; a village that hides a murderer may be punished along with him. So people, especially commoners, are loath to help a criminal. Harsh as it seems, it works.

The vendetta

In some lands, such as Kozakura, the vendetta is officially allowed, and it is a required part of a samurai's honor: when a relative is murdered or killed in a duel, the surviving family must track down and kill the slayer. Special rules apply:

  • The avenger can't be of higher rank than the slain. The eldest son of a samurai family can't avenge a younger brother (he outranks him), and a daimyo's direct retainer can't lawfully avenge a lesser retainer.
  • The avenger must be released from his lord's service: he asks permission, and if the lord thinks the cause just and doesn't need him at the moment, he releases him. When the vendetta is over, he may return to his lord's service with no penalty, and may have gained renown and approval for acting honorably.
  • When he finds his quarry, he must get the local government's approval. This is usually given without question, but may be refused if the quarry is valuable to, or a friend of, the local lord. Acting without approval, he can be arrested for murder.
  • With every approval given, he can challenge his quarry to a duel to the death at any time. Since all is lawful, the winner isn't charged with murder. Either side may have any number of seconds to help; it needn't be one against one.

Source: OA p.141 (Manners; Names). Rewritten in plain words.

Manners

Gajin notice that people here are, as a rule, extraordinarily polite, often taking great pains to behave correctly. Among the upper classes, bad manners are almost as great a crime as murder, and severe punishments can fall on anyone who knowingly commits a social blunder. Correct manners mark the differences between classes and, perhaps more importantly, keep a person from embarrassing himself in public, for there may be no greater sin than being laughed at.

  • The bow is the most obvious courtesy. It isn't just a greeting; it measures respect. Inferiors bow lower to superiors than superiors do to them, and a high official may barely nod to those below him.
  • The kowtow (kneeling and touching the head to the floor) is the greatest deference, normally only before emperors and very powerful lords, but sometimes needed to apologize or beg forgiveness. Except before a powerful lord, it is an extreme act, a person's debasement and surrender to another.
  • Words: remarks, even in jest, can insult. Comments on someone's honor, courage, dislikes, fears, family, dress, behavior, friends, even his possessions can give offense, and insults are seldom taken lightly. A truly generous person might let one or two jests pass, but surely no more. So conversation is often stiff, or worded with extreme politeness to avoid offense.
  • Honor: concern over insults to honor and fear of public ridicule drive much of this politeness, so the DM may take honor from characters who do things that bring ridicule or make them look foolish. Characters can't be careless; they must watch everything they do and say.

Names

Among gajin, a person keeps his given name for life; nicknames and aliases come and go, but changing a name can be a complicated legal matter, implying a new family and identity. In the Eastern Lands, a person can expect to use at least two names in his life, often more, each valid at a given age or situation, plus aliases when he wants to hide who he is. Players needn't have every kind, and many (such as a childhood name) are dropped when a new one is given.

  • Secret name: given at birth and never revealed, supposedly known only to the gods. Superstition holds that learning a person's secret name gives magical power over him.
  • Childhood name: given at birth and used day to day. Childhood names are distinctly different from adult names, so it is easy to tell whether someone has come of age.
  • Adult name: given at coming of age, showing the person is now a full adult with all the rights and duties. After that the childhood name is seldom if ever used.
  • Family name: a hereditary name used with the personal name, generally only among the upper classes and nobles. For lower classes to add a family name is thought insulting and above their station.
  • Clan or tribe name: identifies the person by his group, used by barbarians, for whom tribe matters greatly.
  • Place name: works much like a family name and is common among commoners, naming the village, district, province or such the person comes from.
  • Nickname: for the same reasons as anywhere: to tell two people of the same name apart, as an honor, or as ridicule.
  • Substitute name for unseemly work: used by people of quality, craftsmen, or those in improper occupations. It is the closest thing to an alias, but doesn't hide who the person is (everyone knows who he is and his station); it only keeps his true name from being tied to the undesirable activity.
  • Artist's name: chosen by a writer, craftsman or other artist, because using his real name might be improper (it might recall some powerful person or family), or to make a poetic allusion (a poet taking a name drawn from a great poet of the past).
  • School name: chosen by an artist, craftsman or warrior to show his tie to a school or master.
  • Religious name: taken on entering the priesthood, showing that the person has cut his ties with his past life and become someone new. It usually has some special meaning in the religion.

This module adds the OA rules to the 1e FRPG system: its races and classes on the character sheet, honor and birth, martial arts, OA proficiencies, shukenja and wu jen spells, OA weapons and armor, magic items, monsters and roll tables. Everything is restated in plain words with the book's numbers. You need the book for its original text.

Turning it on

  • Switch the module on in Manage Modules, then accept the offer to build the OA compendia. They can be rebuilt at any time from Configure Settings, 1e FRPG: OA, Rebuild OA compendia (this replaces the copies in the world).
  • The world setting OA races and classes only (on by default) takes the PHB and UA races and classes out of the character lists. Characters already using them keep working. Turn it off to allow gajin characters (see Gajin in The Eastern Lands).

On the character sheet

  • Races: human, korobokuru, hengeyokai and the three spirit folk, with the OA class limits and ability ranges.
  • Classes: barbarian, bushi, kensai, monk, ninja, samurai, shukenja, sohei, wu jen and yakuza, with their experience tables, hit dice, attacks, saving throws and spell tables. Kensai and monk armor class, bushi armor class improvement, monk movement, barbarian constitution hit points, wu jen +1 hit point per die, ninja split-class hit points and the ninja backstab multiplier are applied automatically.
  • OA tab: honor, family honor and birth rank (with a Roll birth button for Table 38), the class abilities for the current level, the proficiency pool, martial arts style and maneuvers, hengeyokai animal form, wu jen spells known and taboos, and yakuza contacts.
  • Proficiencies from the OA Proficiencies compendium use their base number: roll that or more on 1d20, +1 per later slot, never needing less than 3.
  • Martial arts: drag a style from the OA Martial Arts compendium to the Weapons list to attack with it.

Things done by hand

  • Armor pieces (OA Table 53): the sheet counts only the best single armor item, so enter the combined armor class of the pieces as an armor class override or a miscellaneous adjustment.
  • Weights: the book prints weights for weapons (Table 49), armor (Table 54) and barding. Everything else is marked "unspecified", meaning no weight is printed; enter one if your table wants it. Animals, vehicles and services don't count toward load.
  • Sohei spells: the system has no sohei mark, so each spell sohei can use says so at the top of its description.
  • Wu jen elements are noted at the top of each wu jen spell.
  • Two-handed weapons: the book marks them in bold on Table 49, but the scan doesn't show which reliably, so they aren't marked (see Weapons).
  • Treasure: Tables 74 to 85 are written out in the Treasure and Magic Items journals; only Table 86 (OA magic items) is a roll table.

Where the book disagrees with itself

Every number was checked against the page images. Where the text and a table disagree, the table is used and both are noted on the page, marked "as printed": for example the yakuza birth modifier (text -5, Table 37 -10), the XP bonus abilities (text against Table 12), the kensai armor class steps (Table 19), and the calligraphy base number (Table 61 says 18, an example says 17).

The module builds these world compendia. Each entry is restated in plain words with the book's numbers and a source page.

  • OA Journals: the rules by topic, in folders: Characters, Classes, Family, Honor and Society, Money and Equipment, Proficiencies, Magic, Combat and Martial Arts, Running the Game, The Eastern Lands, and this Using This Module folder.
  • OA Spells: 311 spells, in folders by class (Shukenja, Wu Jen) and level. Spells on both lists appear in each, with the level for that list.
  • OA Weapons, Armor and Equipment: 265 items: weapons, missile weapons, ninja weapons, ammunition and armor with their Table 49-54 numbers, and the Table 47 gear (clothing, livestock, miscellaneous equipment, provisions, religious items, services, tack and harness, transport). Ammunition is matched to its weapons (arrows, light and heavy quarrels, bullets, stones and blowgun darts).
  • OA Martial Arts: the four Table 68 styles and the 37 Table 70 special maneuvers, in folders by method.
  • OA Proficiencies: 55 peaceful proficiencies (common, artisan, court and barbarian), with slots and base numbers.
  • OA Magic Items: the 34 Table 86 items. Items with charges roll them once when added to a character.
  • OA Monsters: 47 creatures, in Spirits and Monsters. The chiang lung and tun mi lung roll hit points by size and age, like the other eastern dragons.
  • OA Tables: 32 roll tables: birth (Tables 38-40), divination and fate (Tables 63 and 65), events (Tables 71-73 and ruins), OA magic items (Table 86), and the encounter tables by terrain.

The encounter tables print results 2 to 20 without naming the dice; they are set to 2d10, which can be changed on each table. Ancestry and birthright use the die from Table 38, which changes with birth rank, so their tables use 1d100 to reach every row.
